He seems to be particularly anxious to ascertain the part taken by the Canadian delegation in the invitation to the Soviet union to enter the League of Nations, and also whether the Canadian delegation had officially met Mr. Litvinoff and had made any arrangements with the Russian delegation. The situation is very simple, and I shall endeavour to satisfy the hon. member's desire for information by a brief and direct statement.
The Canadian delegation believed that the movement for the entrance of the Soviet union into the League of Nations, which was initiated by France and supported by the United Kingdom, was in the interest of the League of Nations and of world peace, and it shared in the steps necessary to bring that about. The Canadian delegation did not have any official meeting with the Russian delegation, and did not discuss or enter into any agreements. Owing to the fact that the Soviet union did not enter the league until nearly the end of the session, their delegates took practically no part in the work of the committees. The only plenary meeting of the assembly at which I was present and which was attended by the Russian delegates was the session on September 18, when the business before the meeting was the admission of the U.S.S.R. into the league; after this had been approved the Russian delegates took their seats in the assembly.

subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the refunding of maturing and callable financial obligations of the Canadian National Railways and for the issue of substituted securities therefor, guaranteed by the dominion, in an amount not exceeding $200,000,000.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
The committee is aware no doubt that from time to time in the past the practice has obtained of taking the power through what might be termed an omnibus bill to refund and to fund the direct obligations of the dominion. This bill is designed to take the same course with respect to the guaranteed obligations, or in other words the obligations of the Canadian National Railways which bear the guarantee of the Dominion of Canada. We are asking authority up to the extent of $200,000,000. As a matter of fact there are maturing this year a limited amount of obligations, of which I shall give the exact amount in a few moments. But there are callable provisions in connection with a number of the issues which would enable us, if the market conditions warranted, to refund in the course of the present year not less than $172,000,000. Of course we would ask for the added sum, in the event of our being able to do the same thing with respect to callable obligations which might arise at the end of the year. I do not think I need dwell upon the wisdom of our refunding where possible and in that way reducing the interest charge in consequence. As a matter of fact in the latter part of last year we had two issues of the Canadian National Railways amounting in all, in round figures, to the sum of $20,500,000.. which were re-financed in the month of December. We were able to refund those with an issue of three per cent securities which, in that one transaction alone, will save the railways and to that extent will save the Dominion of Canada not less than $200,000 a year in interest.
To-morrow there falls due an issue of $17,000,000 of four and a half per cent guaranteed Canadian Northern Railway bonds. We have made arrangements temporarily to refund those upon a two pel cent basis. But TMr. H. A. Stewart.]
as the market presents an opportunity we will fund those for a longer term, saving a substantial sum in interest as against the rate which the maturing issues bear. It is necessary of course to secure this authority in advance, because there is not only the question of parliament being in session only for a limited period but the other point, namely, that the majority if not all of these issues are payable in the alternative, either in London, New York or in Canada, at the option of the holder. It would be dependent upon conditions from time to time as to whether a favourable opportunity will present itself.
To show how important it is that we should refund in terms of dollars, may I say that if we are able to refund the total amount which we can refund through the callable provisions, and also because of the obligations maturing to-morrow, during the course of the year, upon a basis comparable to the existing interest rate, we will be able to effect a saving in interest alone of, in round figures, the sum of $2,500,000 a year.

Mr. Chairman, it was
formerly the practice I think for the national railways to issue these obligations on their own account, guaranteed by the federal government. In view of the fact disclosed before the parliamentary committee on national railways and shipping that bonds issued direct by the government could be sold just a little more advantageously than those issued by the national railways direct, and guaranteed by the government, I would like to ask whether it is the intention of the government to have this issued as a direct obligation of the federal government, and charged I presume against the national railways, instead of being issued by the railways, as formerly, and guaranteed by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a very large question. I would not wish to shield myself behind the usual and quite proper formula that the intention of the government can only properly be made known when it has arrived at a decision. I do not take that ground at all. I would point out that it is a large question of policy as to how far it may be wise for the government to add direct obligations in place of their present indirect obligations, especially -bearing in mind the -circumstance that, while it is true there is a margin of difference in the rate on a direct obligation and a guaranteed obligation, the tendency is for that margin to narrow very closely. That is particularly so in Canada. The tendency heretofore has been for that margin to be slightly larger in Great Britain and in New York, but on the whole the tendency has been for that margin to narrow to a very small point. At the moment I would not like to express an opinion whether, on balance, if it were possible, it would be the part of wisdom to stand directly under the whole load at the present time.

speechtext: The minister in referring to some issues that were maturing stated that some were payable in New York and some in London. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I did not get the latter
part of my hon. friend's question.

subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
I asked whether in
future all issues of a similar nature would be payable in Canada only, where possible, or whether the old policy of having them payable both in London and New York, or one or the other, would be continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: The answer to that question would be, which is the more favourable market when an issue is being made? We cannot project ourselves into the future. Every one of the issues

The bill will no doubt

terms of similar bills which have been introduced, and it will provide in the alternative either for direct obligation or for guarantee.

subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may we take it for granted that none of these new issues will be made payable in foreign funds except such as are renewals of maturing issues now payable in foreign funds?

But when it comes to a question of refunding maturities which are held outside of Canada the question of repatriation arises, and it is a question then of what is on balance the wiser policy to pursue.

subtopic: REFUNDING OF MATURING AND CALLABLE FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
In connection with the
minister's last remarks I submit that it is better to pay the Canadian people a higher rate of interest and maintain your obligation in Canada, where it is possible to do so, rather than enter into an obligation in some foreign country. We know that there is considerable money for investment in Canada to-day, even although the banks have invested in government securities over 50 per cent of the savings of the people. I think the government should give very serious consideration to the issue of Canadian obligations, where it is at all possible, even if the rate of interest may be a little higher at the time.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS

speechtext:
Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for the collection by the dominion government of dues to be applied towards the maintenance of the lighthouses and buoy erected or placed by the British government on or near the coasts of the Bahamas and Leeward islands, from ships arriving at and departing from ports in Canada which derive benefits from the said lighthouses and buoy.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
It is impossible for us to obtain
full information before the resolution goes into committee regarding the payment of dues by Canadian or Australian or other vessels that benefit by the lights in question. I suggest we go into committee so that the minister can give us some details.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (South Cape Breton) in the chair.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: With whom did this idea originate? Is it the result of an agreement arrived at by an imperial conference in London; is it by agreement between the dominions and Great Britain; or whence has the idea come which is embodied in this resolution?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the other dominions would adopt similar legislation. He mentioned Australia-

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Yes.

And South Africa, I
thought, and he even mentioned India. Does the minister mean that these dominions or possessions or whatever they are called have ships that pass through that particular territory covered by the resolution?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I cannot say offhand whether those countries have ships deriving benefit from the lights by passing through the Bahamas; but if a ship, British or foreign, navigates in that neighbourhood and thus derives benefit from the lights and does not visit any port in Great Britain, Northern Ireland or the Irish Free State, that ship will not contribute to the maintenance and improvement of those lights although it has benefited from them. That is why the British authorities have asked the dominions to collect dues for the general fund from those ships which do not visit ports on the other side but which visit dominion ports before or after having benefited from those lights; according to regulations it is one penny per ton of registered tonnage of each ship.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: My point is this-perhaps the minister cannot supply the information- but I would like to know if it intended that the other dominions are to enact legislation covering the Bahamas and Leeward islands, or is this to be restricted to Canada? I do not think Australia is interested in it.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I have already stated that all the dominions and colonies were asked to adopt similar legislation, that is to provide for the collection in their ports of dues for the British general fund. I have just stated that the Commonwealth of Australia, India and the Irish Free State have already adopted and probably New Zealand at its forthcoming session will adopt similar legislation; that is, they will become collecting agents for the British general lighthouse fund.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Is this proposal not going to bring about a very serious change in the system which prevails in Canada so far as lighthouses and buoys are concerned? It is very well known that vessels coming into Canadian ports at present have no dues to pay in connection with the maintenance or repair of lighthouses and buoys. According to this resolution if the proposed legislation is put into effect, vessels entering Canadian ports will have to pay to Canada dues which they are not at present called upon to pay. This is a material change and I am afraid it is opening the door to a new policy here which may lead us sooner or later to the establishment of the system which prevails in England and other countries with the exception of Canada and the United States. Is the minister not somewhat afraid that this bill will create a precedent which may prove harmful to our ports later on?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
As I told the house a minute ago, these dues are for the British general fund, not for our own. We are not 
legislating for Canada; we are legislating only to give power to our customs officers to collect for Great Britain dues from ships which do not visit their ports on the other side but which derive benefits from those lighthouses, and visit the Canadian ports. This is only the enforcement of a British law in a British possession, the West Indies; that is all. We are only becoming the collecting agents. No principle in regard to our own legislation is involved. We have no lighthouse dues in this country and so far as I can see we do not intend to impose any dues for lighthouse maintenance. This is to help the British general fund by collecting its lighthouse dues.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Vessels entering Canadian ports have not so far been called upon to pay any dues even to England or to any other country for the maintenance of these lighthouses and buoys, but when the proposed legislation is put on the statute books vessels will have to pay in Canada dues that they formerly were not asked to pay.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Not for our lighthouses. Our officers are only the collecting agents of Great Britain.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: If I understood the minister aright a moment ago, he said that possibly part of these dues will be for our benefit.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I said that perhaps Great Britain will pay us a certain percentage of these dues to cover the expense of collection. That would be only fair.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Has any request been made of the United States government in turn to share part of the expense in the maintenance of these facilities for the same reason the minister gives for asking us, namely that their ships use those ports and receive some services from those lighthouses and buoys? The proposal seems to me eminently fair that one pays on the basis of the service secured, but to be fair it must apply to all parties participating in the benefit. If Canada, Australia and New Zealand are to assume their share of the burden without any foreign countries also sharing, that is not an equitable distribution of the cost. Has the minister any information on that question?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
I am not aware that the United States ever asked for contributions for their lighthouse services, but I can say that United States vessels navigating through the Bahamas and Leeward islands, if they do not visit a port in Great Britain or Northern Ireland or the Irish Free State but visit a port in Canada, they will be asked by our officers to pay these dues.

Aids to Navigation-Collection oj Dues

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: But they will not necessarily visit a port in Canada. They may be plying between United States ports and ports in the Bahamas. Why should they not in turn be required to pay part of the cost? Why should the United States customs authorities not be induced by voluntary arrangement to collect just as we are now being asked to collect some share of the cost?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: So far Great Britain has asked only its dominions and colonies to help it in the collection of these dues.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: This is going to be to the detriment of Canadian ports. After this proposed legislation is passed, vessels entering Canadian ports will have to pay these dues. If the same vessels visit United States ports, they will have nothing to pay for the use of these lighthouses and sendees. That appears to be a system which will operate against our Canadian ports.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: There may be a loss to the British general lighthouse fund if they have no agreement with the United States for the collection of dues in the ports of that country, but at the present time Great Britain is asking the aid of the dominions and colonies only in the collection of these dues.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
I quite understand that
what we are creating here is a collecting agency for England, but I am afraid it is going to operate to the detriment of our Canadian ports. It is going to impose dues on all vessels visiting our ports.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Vessels which have
derived benefit from those lights.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Certainly, but vessels also deriving benefits from those lights going into the United States will have nothing to pay.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: They will not be encouraged to come to Canada, they will go to the United States.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
I think the best thing the
minister can do with this resolution is to let it stand. It is quite evident that he is badly advised either by the British government or by his officials in putting this resolution on the order paper. I could understand it if, following the Prime Minister's wish regarding conventions about eight-hour days and minimum wages and other matters for the whole British empire, or the whole world, the British government were putting forth a proposition that all lights in the British empire should come under one general fund. If that were
the proposal then I could understand why ships coming into Canada or going from Canada should pay into that fund. But why in the name of heaven should any ship either coming to or going from Canada pay for lights in the Bahamas or the Leeward islands? Do the Bahamas pay for our lights in Canada? Do the Leeward islands, the Windward islands, does Australia? And the minister tells us that the Irish Free State has agreed to pay; have they any shipping? You might as well say that Switzerland or Alberta is willing to agree to collect for these islands.
Mr. MoINTOSH: What about Saskatchewan?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Or Saskatchewan. The thing
is ridiculous. The minister knows that the Canadian taxpayers pay for all the lights on both our coasts and on the great lakes. We do not ask the Bahamas or the Leeward islands or Australia or the Irish Free State or even Great Britain to help pay for these lights. Not only does Canada pay for all the lights in Canada but also for some in Newfoundland as the minister knows. These are lights of a particular kind and placed in positions of particular advantage for Canadian and other shipping. But why should the Canadian vessel owner or taxpayer pay for lights in the Bahamas or the Leeward islands? Take for example the Empress of Britain, she makes perhaps twenty trips to Quebec in a year. If this resolution passes, every time she enters at Quebec she will have to pay lights dues for lights, where? Down at Nassau. The only time the Empress of Britain goes to Nassau is perhaps once a year; when liquor gets scarce in Quebec and she takes a number of passengers down to Nassau. Mr. Chairman, the suggestion or resolution is ridiculous. I say seriously to the minister that when Great Britain comes forward with a proposition that all the lights in the British empire should be maintained from one fund that will be time enough to ask Canadian shipping to help keep up lights in the Bahamas or on the coast of England or elsewhere.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
I would be opposed to
that.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: So would I, but I am putting that forward as a much better proposition than the one the minister asks us to adopt now. I ask the minister to have the committee rise, so as at least to give time for more consideration.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
I look on the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) as the admiral of the Canadian navy. I trust

the day is not far distant when Canada may realize its duty to the British fleet, and be ready not only to contribute to aids to navigation but to make a proper contribution by the people of Canada to maritime freedom. We do not know what we owe to the British fleet. When the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough was sitting on this side of the house he will remember the Petersen contracts in which it was proposed to pay thousands of dollars by way of subsidy to a concern with no control over ocean rates at all. I hope the day is not far distant when the people of Quebec and of all the provinces will take a broad view of this matter, because I believe in the principle on which confederation is based, the principle of all for one and one for all. My friends on the other side are always talking about more overseas trade. We have the Canadian merchant marine and it is necessary no doubt to maintain these contributions and collections as aids to navigation, and they have not been opposed in the past by hon. members opposite. I maintain that not only should there be a contribution towards aids to navigation, to avoid disasters and loss of life, but it should be made willingly. I hope the day is not far distant when these aids may be extended and increased to the head of the great lakes, where there have been many disasters through lack of proper lights and signals and aids to navigation. I commend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) for the resolution. Hon. members of the opposition should be consistent.
I have never gone to sea but if I went I should feel safe with such a sea admiral as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: It took a great deal of circumlocution or circumnavigation and ingenuity for the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) to reach the point where he could wave the flag and sing Britannia Rules the Waves. But with all respect to him I think we have a perfect right to object to this resolution until at least we have more information. The minister has told us that the Irish Free State and Australia and India are proposing to pass similar legislation.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
They have passed
similar legislation, they are collecting these dues.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
He has not yet told us who asked this country to do so. Was it by a letter from the British government, a letter from the collectors of the lighthouse fund, or is it a matter of agreement, one of these conventions that we are ratifying now, or did it IMr. Church.]
originate in the minds of officials in his department? We want far more light, but we do not want to pay for it unless we have to. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) referred to the tax on vessels such as the Empress of Britain. The Empress of Britain I think is a vessel of about forty thousand tons. I understood the minister to say that the tax would be a penny a ton each time this vessel comes into Quebec?

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I understand the tonnage of the Empress of Britain is forty-two thousand tons, and the tax is a penny a ton on the registered tonnage.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: That would amount to $420 each time this vessel came into Quebec.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: It would be $840.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I am not surprised that the Prime Minister needs an economic council, when the whole House of Commons cannot make a simple calculation in multiplication. I am inclined to agree with the Prime Minister that it is $840. Therefore that is what it would cost the Empress of Britain every time she came into the port of Quebec if the explanation given by the minister is correct. And she comes in something like ten or twelve times a season.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: No, twenty times.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
It has been pointed out that the Empress of Britain may conceivably go to the Bahamas once a year with one of those ocean cruises, and for that she would have to pay something like $8,000 or $9,000. The thing seems absurd on the face of it. As has been pointed out by some of our friends from the prairies it seems absurd that we should carry the burden of these duties when the United States, our next-door neighbour, is exempt. And particularly may I say that it is with a certain amount of regret I see this government, of all governments, imposing such dues on vessels coming into Canadian ports. One of the principal articles in the program of this government was free ports, though I must say that in the application of that term I fear those who preached that we should have free ports in this country neglected to look up either the dictionary meaning of the term or the meaning generally accepted in maritime countries. However, they left the impression with the people of this country that free ports meant ports with lower dues, but here one of the first pieces of legislation with respect to ports will place our ports at a disadvantage as compared with those of the United States.

Aids to Navigation-Collection oj Dues
And for whose benefit is this being done? It is for the benefit of ships trading in the Bahamas, for the benefit of ships, I would say, largely owned by Americans. I do not know what the proportion is, but I would say that far more ships of American registry ply in those waters than ships of Canadian or even of British registry.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: We have only two ships in Canada that go to the Bahamas.

subtopic: BAHAMAS AND LEEWARD ISLANDS-COLLECTION OF DUES TO APPLY TOWARDS MAINTENANCE BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT OF SHIPPING SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Apart from bootlegging
vessels we have probably only two Canadian ships that go to the Bahamas. My hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough tells me the only tiwo vessels are the Lady Rodney and the Lady Somers. It strikes me that the whole proposition is very much like having the American government ask us to impose an income tax on our citizens, the proceeds of which would be devoted to keeping up the highways or bridges of the United States, and more than that, it would be the imposition of a tax on people formerly exempt, because in this case vessels coming into Canada, as has been shown here this afternoon, are exempt from dues in connection with our own lighthouses. I cannot imagine anything more extraordinary than asking the Canadian people, who have contributed largely over a period of years to the cost of lighthouses and other aids to navigation, and who do not charge that cost to vessels entering Canadian ports, now to suffer in any way or make any further sacrifices in order to keep up the lighthouses of any other country. I cannot understand why this legislation should be introduced, and after mature consideration I think probably the minister will withdraw it.
Mr. VEiNilOT: Will the minister explain how these dues are collected now? How does the British government get any revenue from vessels using or deriving benefits from the Bahamas islands lighthouses?
Mr. DURlAlNLBAU: The collection is made when a ship that has benefited by tho.se lights visits a British port, and similar laws have been adopted by Australia, India and other parts of the British empire. If a ship does not visit a British port before or after having derived benefits from those lights but lands in a Canadian port, under the proposed legislation the collection will be made at this port. That will foe the practice in Canada if this legislation is adopted. At the present time if a Canadian ship derives benefits from those lighthouses on its way to Great Britain, for instance, she pays these dues on her arrival in the British port. subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 12, consideration of the motion of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. 8, to establish an unemployment and social insurance commission, to provide for a national employment service, for insurance against unemployment, for aid to unemployed persons, and for other forms of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I must say that I am a supporter of the principle of unemployment insurance. I, with other members on this side of the house, have always approved of it every time the question has been discussed or raised in this house. Unemployment insurance is no new move; if did not come as a 'bolt from the blue as the result of a certain atmospheric commotion one fine evening last January. It has been in force in many countries for different periods of time. The World Economic Survey for 1934, published by the League of Nations, mentions that this form of insurance is now in force in seventeen countries. In nine countries it is a compulsory system, while in eight countries it is voluntary. The United States magazine, Review of Reviews, in its January edition mentions that at present unemployment insurance schemes are being discussed in forty-eight states in the world, as well as in the congress of the United States.
In England unemployment insurance was established in 1911, after a few years of work. There it constituted part of the chain of social policies launched by the late Mr. Asquith when he was Prime Minister, after the elections of 1906, and it was presented to the House of Commons in England by Mr. Lloyd George, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, after a thorough study of the question in Germany, where the' system was already in force. Indeed, it was a part of their social program of reforms, which included old age pensions, health insurance, factory acts, a companies act, and wage regulation acts. All these were put on the statute books of Great Britain by the Asquith government, which tends to show that those men, the Liberals of Great Britain, who are sometimes charged with being adepts at the policy of laissez-faire, are those who put most of the social legislation of England on the statute books of that country.
This is no radical change in the capitalist system, I assure you. Some of the nations which have the system in force are the strongest bulwarks of capitalism, and Canada is far ahead of them in the matter of advanced legislation. Nowhere has it cured unemployment ; especially has it not solved the problem of a depression unemployment, such as
I Mr. MacNicol.]
exists at the present time. This measure cannot help those1 who are unemployed in Canada to-day. The government are rather unfortunate in their chain of reform legislation. They introduce the eight hour day bill at a time when the workers of Canada would like to work one day a week if they could; they introduce a bill to enforce a day of rest every week when the workmen would1 like to have an enforced day of labour weekly, and they introduce an unemployment insurance bill which may give something in the future to the labour men of Canada who at the present time can afford to contribute to the fund, which most of them cannot. It is, I admit, a sop to discontent. Accompanied by other legislation which would deal with the present distressing problem of unemployment this legislation would be desirable, and because I am in favour of it I wish we might have this system as a valid, constitutional instrument, and not merely what is proposed by the government to-day.
Let me tell my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that I agree with him that it is desirable that this should foe a national system. There would be objections to various different provincial schemes of unemployment insurance instead of a national scheme. For instance, it would disturb the equilibrium of industrial relations in the various provinces. Labour naturally would be inclined to go to the provinces where such legislation was on the statute books, and on the other hand it is possible that employers would prefer provinces where they would not be forced to contribute to such a scheme. So it is desirable that it should be a national scheme. I agree with the view taken -by members of the government until they changed their opinion in January last; a national scheme should be reached by either an amendment to the British North America Act, by some enabling: legislation on the part of the provinces or by some understanding with the provinces in order to establish a scheme which would be acceptable to everyone in this country.
A constitutional aspect was raised on various, occasions in this house by the members of the government. There was the question of property and civil rights, which no one can. deny not only enters into the discussion of this matter but is the mainstay of the whole proposal. The scheme relates to relations between employers and employees, and more so when it is a compulsory scheme, as the one: which we are discussing to-day.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Lapointe
How has the government tried to get around this difficulty? I was hoping my right hon. friend opposite would give some further explanations when he moved the second reading of the 'bill. When speaking on the resolution he said that he did not want to anticipate the longer explanations he would give when the bill was under discussion. My right hon. leader has raised the question, and I was hoping some member of the government would give the house the reasons upon which they base their new found claim to jurisdiction in the matter. However, not having received that, I must rely on the preamble of the bill, a very long preamble in which the government tries to find justification for the legislation mainly on two points, first on sections 23 and 427 of the treaty of peace and secondly on the provision of peace, order and good government of Canada.
As I am limited 'to forty minutes in my observations I am afraid I have not the time to make complete quotations. However article 23 states that the memibens of the league:
(a) will endeavour to secure and maintain fair and humane conditions of labour for men, women and children, both in their own countries and in all countries to -which their commercial and industrial relations extend, and for that purpose will establish and maintain the necessary international organizations;
But they do not specify the manner of doing so. Subsection (a) is preceded by two lines which qualify the whole article:
Subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon.
The article I have read is subject to the qualification that the whole arrangement is subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon.
Then article 427, the last article in the labour part of the treaty, merely enunciates a principle. It states:
The high contracting parties recognizing that the well-being, physical, moral and intellectual, of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance, have framed, in order to further this great end, the permanent machinery provided for in section 1 and associated with that of the League of Nations. They recognize that differences of climate, habits and customs of economic opportunity and industrial tradition,-
-enter into a consideration of the case. I have not the time to read it all. Then they continue:
But holding as they do, that labour should not be regarded merely as an article of commerce. they think that there are methods and principles- for regulating labour conditions
which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
Then they indicate nine goals as being desirable to reach,-the eight hour day, the weekly day of rest, the abolition of child labour, and so on. But unemployment insurance is not even mentioned in the goals which are outlined to the nations of the world as being desirable. The article concludes by stating:
Without claiming that these methods and principles are either complete or final, the high contracting parties are of opinion that they are well fitted to guide the policy of the League of Nations.
And so on. Where do we find there' an obligation to enact employment insurance legislation? I do not wish to enter upon the same line of argument I used a few days ago in connection with another matter, but I repeat that it is only the obligation which creates the jurisdiction in favour of this parliament.
Section 132 of the British North America Act reads as follows:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
There must be obligations binding on Canada as a result of conventions or treaties with foreign countries which bind Canada. I am surprised to find the following words in the preamble of the bill:
And whereas it is desirable to discharge the obligations to Canadian labour assumed under the provisions of the said treaty.
To discharge obligations of Canada to Canadian labour is a noble act, but it is not covered by section 132. What gives jurisdiction to this parliament is the obligation of Canada towards foreign countries, not towards any class of the population in Canada. It is not stated in the preamble that Canada had any obligations towards foreign countries as a result of sections 23 and 427 of the peace treaty. My hon. friends cannot even argue that there is a draft convention, as they did in connection with the eight hour day. There are draft conventions but for a reason better known to the Prime Minister they have not been approved by the house, have not been laid on the table of the house and can give no authority or jurisdiction to parliament. I need not deal with that part of the question at all.
How could Canada be bound to an unemployment insurance scheme? There are 50 member nations of the League of Nations who

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Lapointe
are obligated by the peace treaty, 66 per cent of whom have no unemployment insurance schemes. I repeat that there is nothing binding, but that a goal has been shown to the members as being desirable.
Then there is the further point, namely the jurisdiction resulting from peace, order and good government. Although I do not wish to repeat what I said a few days ago I should like to read part of section 91 of the British North America Act:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and' with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
And in most of the decisions of the privy council regarding jurisdiction which have gone against the contention of the federal parliament it has been specially stated-and the matter is so clearly expressed in the section there can be no doubt-that those laws for the peace, order and good government must be in relation to matters not coming within the classes of subjects assigned to the legislatures. Surely property and civil rights are one subject which is specifically assigned exclusively to the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act.
I shall not refer again to the various decisions of the privy council except perhaps to the Snider case in 1925 where one of the tests of provincial jurisdiction was that the matter of industrial disputes was one that could be dealt with separately by any province, and however desirable it would be to have national legislation with regard to it the fact that it could be dealt with by any province took away the claim to jurisdiction set forth by the federal parliament. Is it not the same in this matter? Does anybody claim that the provinces would not have the right to have an unemployment insurance scheme of their own? Obviously they have that right. Nobody can challenge that, and because of that, the thing cannot be changed into a federal matter merely by a stroke of the pen here, by the will of the government.
My hon. friends opposite rely on the two aviation and radio cases. The judgment in the first was delivered in November of 1931, and the judgment in the second on the ninth of February, 1932. I do not want to discuss this thing over and over again except to say that in both cases there was a binding convention; there was a treaty in respect to aviation, and there was a convention in respect to radio signed by ninety countries and ratified by His Majesty the King. Canada was bound

by the provisions of those two treaties, and those were the reasons for the judgments that were delivered.
I do not want to quote any of the remarks of the judge except one. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, at page 642 of Hansard of February 8, 1935, quoted the remarks of the Lord Chancellor in the aviation case, but obviously he was .led astray by the officers or the secretaries who looked up the quotations for him because between two paragraphs there has been eliminated a most important one which changes the whole complexion, and I should say the whole meaning of the quotation. I am going to read what was eliminated and I hope that anybody who reads my right hon. friend's speech that was delivered on Friday last will insert these words in the quotation on page 642 at the bottom of the second column where the three dots are. The quotation I am going to read is more voluble than the three dots:
Inasmuch as the act embodies a compromise under which the original provinces agreed to federate, it is important to keep in mind that the preservation of the rights of minorities was a condition on which such minorities entered into the federation, and the foundation upon which the whole structure was subsequently erected. The process of interpretation as the years go on ought not to be allowed to dim or to whittle down the provisions of the original contract upon which the federation was founded nor is it legitimate that any judicial construction of the provisions of sections 91 and 92 should enforce a new and a different contract upon the federating bodies.
That disposes of the claim that because Canada in common with the rest of the world has widened her activities and developed tremendously, it follows that the British North America Act also has widened and developed and should be changed. It is true that Canada has developed and has widened her activities. But the British North America Act is as it was, and until it is amended in the proper way, which I do not oppose, I say to the government that the only way for this legislation to be enacted as they are trying to do, without the cooperation of the provinces, is by an amendment to the British North America Act. But so long as that act remains there, it is our constitution, and there is no widening process nor development that can change it without new action on the part of those who agree to changing it.
The right hon. the Prime Minister in introducing the resolution said that the law officers of the crown are of the opinion that this legislation is within the jurisdiction of this parliament. Well, if that is so, they have changed their minds, for on the tenth

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Lapointe
of May, 1928, in the committee presided over by my hon. friend from North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) the Deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. Edwards, was heard, and I quote these three words from his remarks:
Mr. Heaps: If I understand the statements here this morning correctly I would interpret your remarks to mean that the federal government has not authority to impose dominionwide legislation, or has not authority to impose compulsory unemployment insurance, or sickness insurance?
And the answer of the Deputy Minister of Justice was:
Yes, that is correct.
On April 23, 1929, the same Mr. Edwards, the Deputy Minister of Justice, was again heard by the same committee, and he referred to his evidence of the preceding year and stated that he adhered to what he had said at that time.
Now I come to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) who is the head of the law officers, and I am going to quote from his remarks in this house on March 22, 1933, and my hon. friend will not be able to say now that he held these views because he had not received or read the judgments in the aviation and radio cases because this was more than a year after the radio case and eighteen months after the aviation case. I quote from pages 3294 and 3295 of Hansard of March 22, 1933:
Mr. Guthrie: As the department over which I have at the moment the honour of presiding is and has been for some time looking into this question of unemployment insurance, may I say a word in regard to the matter. The difficulties in the way of a federal system of unemployment insurance are very serious if such a system is to be carried out on a contributory basis which, I believe, is the only method which would be approved by parliament, that is, contributions by employees, by employers, by the federal treasury and perhaps as well by the provincial treasuries. To inaugurate and carry out a scheme of that kind without provincial consent and without an amendment to the British North America Act would be impossible. Parliament cannot force employers to contribute nor can it force employees to contribute. These are matters entirely within the jurisdiction of the various provinces, and unless the provinces are willing to surrender some of their rights, their powers, it is impossible without an amendment to the British North America Act to carry out any scheme under the jurisdiction of this parliament. I noticed the leader of the opposition stated in his opening remarks that it would be just as easy to carry out an unemployment insurance scheme as to carry out on old age pension plan.
Mr. Mackenzie King: No. I said the very reverse; I said that it would not be as easy
to carry out an unemployment insurance scheme.
Mr. Guthrie: That is the corrected opinion of my right hon. friend after the Minister of Labour had spoken.
Mr. Mackenzie King: No, it is not. With all deference to my hon. friend, if he will look at the record, he will see that I said that the same questions of jurisdiction and methods of procedure arise in each case.
Mr. Guthrie: The same questions do not arise. In the old age pension scheme the question was simply this: the federal government will contribute certain money and the provincial governments will contribute certain money. The difficulty was overcome by a dominion act and a provincial act. That was all there was to the matter. This plan of unemployment insurance involves not only the question of government contribution, but compulsory contributions by employers and employees, which is a matter of purely provincial jurisdiction.
I am disclosing no secret when I say that at the conference the provinces were not prepared to give up those rights nor to agree to any amendment to the British North America Act for that purpose. Very serious discussions took place, and while the question was advanced, it certainly was not advanced to the point of agreement, no agreement being reached on the subject. Until we have a solution of these two questions: the power to assess the employer and the power to assess the employee, I do not think there is much hope of a federal unemployment insurance scheme. If we can overcome those difficulties; if we can reach an arrangement upon those two questions, then I think the field is fairly clear and satisfactory legislation can be formulated. But until we have those questions cleared up. I do not think very much advance can be made.
That was the opinion of the Minister of Justice, expressed in March, 1933, and the leader of the opposition has quoted statements to the same effect, made by the Prime Minister on two occasions, on April 29, 1931, and on November 22, 1932-all, except the 1931 remarks, after the two judgments on radio and aviation. But there is more than that on the part of the Prime Minister. There is his letter, dated August 31, 1934, to the provincial premiers, in which the question of unemployment insurance is raised. I will read three or four of the first paragraphs of that letter:
As I indicated at the meeting with the provincial premiers in July last, it is my purpose to call a conference of representatives of the governments of all the provinces to meet at Ottawa before the end of the year to discuss with the federal government the following questions and' such other matters as may be placed upon the agenda after I have been advised of the views of the premiers of the several provinces:
1.	What steps can be taken to reduce the evils of duplicate taxation and provide a more logical allocation of sources of revenue now available to dominion and provinces?

2.	Are the provinces prepared to surrender their exclusive jurisdiction over legislation dealing with such social problems as old age pensions, unemployment and social insurance, hours and conditions for work, minimum wages, et cetera, to the dominion parliament? If so, on what terms and conditions?
3.	Is it desirable to endeavour more clearly to define the respective jurisdiction of the dominion parliament and provincial legislatures with respect to health and agricultural and other matters in which there is a duplication of effort by federal and provincial authorities?
I have not time to read it all, but my right hon. friend said the other day that when he wrote paragraph 2 he was speaking-

Well, the whole letter then-he was speaking for the provinces; he -was stating the case of the provinces. My right hon. friend in paragraph 2 says:
Are the provinces prepared to surrender their exclusive jurisdiction over legislation dealing with such social problems as old age pensions, unemployment and social insurance, hours and conditions for work, minimum wages, et cetera to the dominion parliament?
And in paragraph 3 he makes this statement:
Is it desirable to endeavour more clearly to define the respective jurisdiction of the dominion parliament and provincial legislatures with respect to health and agricultural and other matters in which there is a duplication of effort by federal and provincial authorities?
Paragraph 2 was referring to matters which are exclusively under the provinces, and No. 3 was referring to concurrent matters on which both the federal and the provincial governments have authority. I invite you, Mr. Speaker, I invite every member of this house, I invite the Dominion of Canada to read this letter and say what other meaning can be attached to what the right hon. gentleman said. And while he was writing that, only a few months ago, my right hon. friend, having stated at almost every session that the matter was purely a provincial one, made the statement on the radio in January that this program of reform he had been unable to deal with because of the storm which had prevailed during these last four years, in which he had to steer the ship. Well, w'as it the storm or the British North America Act which was the obstacle in the way of this reform legislation? It appears, by every declaration, not only by the Prime Minister, but by the Minister of Justice, by the Deputy Minister of Justice and by other members of the cabinet, by the Secretary of State, that the constitution was the obstacle that was in the way. The Secretary of State, who is a very distinguished lawyer, spoke in 
Montreal before the Young Men's Canadian Club at the Queens hotel in November last, when he absolutely took the stand that these matters are exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The Secretary of State uses energetic language at times and I like him for that. Let me read his concluding words:
On the other hand, there are political and social propagandists-blind leaders of the blind -who are persistent in their efforts to procure the dominion parliament to pretend to appropriate and illegally to exercise powers which are exclusively vested in the provincial government. One of these, to whom I recently suggested that a certain course of action was unconstitutional, made reply: "To hell with the constitution!"
I apologize to you, Mr. Speaker.
In these days of social unrest, when people who are suffering are insistent on reform and impatient of delay, those who believe that evolution is more effective than revolution must again and again and persistently demand that municipal authorities assume their full responsibilities in municipal matters, provincial authorities assume their full responsibilities in provincial matters, and dominion authorities there full responsibility in dominion matters.
It is a proper matter for intelligent discussion as to whether the exclusive power of the provinces in matters of social reform should be considerably curtailed, and the powers of the dominion correspondingly extended. Meanwhile, until the British North America Act is amended by constitutional methods, no good purpose can be served by either the dominion parliament or the provincial legislatures attempting illegally to exercise powers now fully vested in the other or others of them.
This is from the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, November 27, 1934. Of course I admit that I have the greatest admiration for my right hon. friend; he is, as we all know, a distinguished jurist, but I have an admiration for his opinions as expressed last year, the year before and the year before that rather than for the one he expresses to-day on the eve of a general election in order to promote a nelw program of reform.
The other day I heard the Minister of Finance, replying to a motion for the nationalization of banks and explaining why the Bank of Canada had not been made entirely publicly owned, say there might be danger on the eve of a general election; the temptations might be great. He said:	Governments are composed of men; they are human and might yield to certain demands to which they would not yield at other times. Perhaps the nearness of the elections has something to do with this ne'W move on the part of the government.
But let me ask this question of my hon. friends opposite. We all say it is desirable that this should be a national system. What

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Lapointe
if some of the provinces, not having been consulted, not having been asked to cooperate, this scheme not having been submitted to them in any way, decide that they will enact their own schemes of unemployment insurance? .Nobody will deny (that they have the right to do so; nobody can say that they have not the right to do so. What will foe the consequence? There will be chaos, confusion; and will that foe advantageous to labour and to the industrial situation of Canada? The government cannot plead emergency on questions of present relief. We have unemployment all over the land. Yesterday I received a letter from the officers of the council of my own city of Quebec pointing out thait the number of people on relief is just as large as it was last year at the same time. We have a problem of relief, and the government might argue that there was an emergency as regards relief for unemployment, but not an emergency for a scheme of unemployment insurance which will be operative only in future years and when probably times will have become normal, more particularly because with such a scheme you cannot solve a problem of unemployment created by depression but can solve only a problem of temporary unemployment created by social conditions or changes in factories where people are employed
My right hon. friend said to the board of trade in Montreal the other day that before he changed his mind on many of these questions he had had conversations with Mr. Litvinoff of Russia, Sir Stafford Cripps and Mr. Strachey.
Mr. BENNETT': That is not correctly reported. I had not conversations with Sir Stafford Cripps, but I said that Sir Stafford Cripps and Mr. Strachey had made speeches in Canada.

I repeat that the only way to deal with this question properly would be either by an amendment to the British North America Act in order to have valid legislation or by passing our legislation after having had an understanding with the provinces by way of enabling legislation or otherwise.
I am sorry my time is short. I should have liked to place on Hansard a quotation from what the Secretary of State said when some hon. members in the far corner in 1932, two years ago, preached that this dominion dhould simply assume jurisdiction as to the water powers of the province of Quebec and deal with them as if we had jurisdiction. This is what he replied:
It is not for me to say that that contention is valid until it is finally passed upon by a judicial court of final appeal. But when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests that we should take that property and that right, leaving the province to contest our taking of its property, that is simply making the appeal which the ordinary burglar-makes when he enters a house and takes property which he knows does not belong to him, leaving it to the householder to put the burglar-out and to protect his chattels. I feel sometimes in sympathy with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he suggests, in regard to the protection of labour in this country, certain social improvements, but that proper end cannot be attained by burglary and theft such as he has advocated' in this house to-night.
That is exactly what the government is doing now. The government know there is a considerable body of public opinion in Canada which says that this is a provincial matter. In addition they know the law officers of the various provinces claim that this is a provincial matter, but they simply say, ego nominor leo-my name is lion; I assume the authority; I am passing the legislation. That is the same psychology as that of a lynching

mob-to assume powers, even when one does not know whether he has them or not. I am sorry I cannot conclude my remarks at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his address the other day gave a number of reasons, or alleged reasons, why he had not proceeded to do during his regime what he so strongly urged this government to do immediately after they took office. The first of those reasons was the financial situation: I shall touch on that very briefly.
The right hon. gentleman said it was necessary to balance the budget and to take care of the obligations of the government before venturing upon any new scheme. The budget was balanced, he tells us, in 1924. From that time on he had various other reasons for not proceeding, to which I shall presently refer. It is remarkable, however, that while the party opposite could not proceed with social legislation because of financial conditions, in the last year of their term of office they were able to authorize the Canadian National Railways to spend $205,000,000. That authorization is remarkable in view of the statement made by the right hon. gentleman on Tuesday last, when he said the following, as reported on page 737- of Hansard:
In order that I may not be misunderstood, may I make clear that if we are to economize, as I think we shall probably be compelled to do all around, the last place at which I think economy should begin is with respect to social services. I think great care should be taken to see that those persons in the country who are less fortunate than their fellowmen are the ones to receive the first concern of the government.
That was the right hon. gentleman's view on Tuesday last. But he could not launch such a scheme as this in 1929, although he could authorize the Canadian National Railways to spend $205,000,000. The next reason he offered was want of jurisdiction. I shall refer to that briefly at the conclusion of my remarks: I pass it for the time being.
The next reason he offered was somewhat akin to the first. He said that very difficult matters were pending between the provinces and the federal government; that in the western provinces the question had arisen respecting the return of the natural resources to the

provinces, and while that was pending he thought it unwise to launch any scheme that would involve a question of jurisdiction as between the dominion and the provinces. He said also that in the east there was the question of maritime rights that had to be settled, and for that reason also he was not prepared to launch any new scheme of social services.
The fourth reason he gave is more remarkable still. He said that during the years 1921 to 1925 he had practically no majority in the house. He said he had a majority of but one. The balance of power then was held by hon. gentlemen who sit to the left of the official opposition, and he said that with that small majority of one it was unsafe for him to launch any measure pertaining to social services. So apparently the responsibility rested upon hon. gentlemen sitting to the left of the official opposition; he did not feel that he could depend upon their support for his social legislation. It is remarkable, though, that the only resolutions dealing with social services during that period, the only moves that were made along that line, emanated from those hon. gentlemen who held the balance of power. Yet while they were urging these resolutions and forcing them upon the attention of the government he was afraid to bring in measures such as these for fear hon. gentlemen to the left of the official opposition would not support measures which they themselves had suggested! It is interesting to note what he said on that subject. At page 740 of Hansard the right hon. gentleman said:
It is one thing to be in a position to bring in extensive schemes on any subject when as prime minister one has behind him a majority of thirty or forty members who at a nod will do as he wishes; it is an entirely different thing to attempt the passage of such measures when a prime minister has for himself and party a majority of only one, or no majority at all.
From that remark I gather he expects when he has a majority of thirty or forty they will obey his will at a nod. Yet we have heard them time and again in this house complain that the government party stands behind its leader, whom they accuse of being a dictator, a Mussolini and all that sort of thing, just because the members who sit with him on this side of the house are prepared to stand behind him to put through the program which the government initiates.
The next reason given by the right hon. gentleman was a yet more remarkable and more vital one. He said, If I did pass this legislation I did not know what the Senate would do. I refer to page 740.

We did hear something before about reforming the Senate, and all the right hon. gentleman had to say at the end of nine years was that the Senate was so bad that he could not do anything on account of it.
The right hon. gentleman made a mistake which is frequently made when a man is making out a case, that of making out too good a case. He said that as far back as 1931 he urged upon the Prime Minister that he should take immediate steps in this matter of unemployment insurance, that he should call a conference of the provinces and try to
get them to agree, and that he should proceed to consider amendments to the British North America Act and to settle once for all the question of jurisdiction. I ask hon. gentlemen to note that that was the right hon. gentleman's first year in opposition. Let us see what he had to say in his last year of power, just a few short months before he made that speech in 1931 to which he referred, in which he urged upon the Prime Minister what he ought to do. I quote now from Hansard of 1930 at page 106. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement of the Prime Minister regarding unemployment insurance, which he made yesterday to a western delegation, will the federal government take the initiative in calling a special conference to consider this problem?
That was a straight question, and the reply was rather remarkable. The Prime Minister of that day, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) said:
Perhaps the hon. member will intimate what that statement was.
Almost twenty-four hours had passed and he had forgotten what he had told the delegation from the west. Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said:
As T understand the statement, it was to the effect that the federal government was very much concerned in the matter of unemployment and believed that one of the solutions was a system of unemployment insurance and that the government would be willing to take any steps possible towards bringing about an understanding between the provinces and the federal government. I want to know if the government will be willing to undertake the calling of a special conference so that this matter can be expedited.
Following that we have the last official pro nouncement by the leader of the opposition when he was in power, as to what he proposed to do in regard to unemployment insurance. Here it is:
My recollection is that a special committee of this house considered this question last session and brought to the house a report to the effect that unemployment insurance was necessarily a matter with which provincial governments rather than the federal government would have to deal. I think I expressed the view yesterday that in my opinion a system of unemployment insurance would be a constructive way to deal with the unemployment problem-
That is a little different from what he is saying to-day.
-to which system not only the employer and the governments concerned would contribute but the worker also.

If the provinces make a move in this matter and it appears that the federal government can be of assistance-
You see, first the provinces were to move, not the Prime Minister.

I shall be obliged if the
hon. gentleman will just keep quiet and let me continue:
If the provinces make a move in this matter and it appears that the federal government can be of assistance in helping to bring about uniformity as between the provinces of any plan proposed, or can cooperate in other ways in any discussion on the subject, we shall be glad upon invitation to take the matter under consideration.
That is the extent to which the right hon. gentleman was prepared to go in 1930, the last year he was in power. Neither he nor his party intended to make a move; they were leaving it to the provinces to formulate a plan and to invite him to come in and, by discussion, help them cooperate between themselves, and he would only come in upon invitation. That is the man who, a few short months later, found that there was a great obligation on the part of the Prime Minister of this country to call conferences, to investigate the jurisdiction in order to settle that question forever and, if necessary, to amend the British North America Act.
I was rather struck with the very fervent and rather poetic peroration of the right hon. gentleman which appears at page 754 of Hansard for this year. Referring to the bill brought in by the Prime Minister the right hon. gentleman said:
In the circumstances, I say to the Prime Minister that in these days of stress and anxiety and suffering for the mass of the people, they are crying for bread and he is giving them a stone. They are crying for fish and he is giving them a serpent-
Those words sounded rather familiar to me; I thought perhaps I might have heard them in some former incarnation, but I discovered that I had heard them in this house. In 1932 the right hon. gentleman made a similar peroration, and at the end of his address in connection with the unemployment and farm relief measure, he said:
The women and children who are suffering in this country to-day have asked the Prime Minister for bread, they have asked him for work, but he has given them not even a stone

or a serpent; he has given them an extinct enactment, he has given them a dead statute.
That was at page 704 of Hansard for 1932. I might suggest to the right hon. gentleman that a man who sees serpents so frequently is in rather a critical state of mind. I might also suggest to the right hon. gentleman that when he .made that statement in 1932 he was belittling the statute then before the house to reinstate the farm relief and unemployment measure of the previous pear. My right hon. friend made the very dramatic statement that the Prime Minister was giving the people a dead statute when they wanted bread. I should just like to recall to his mind the fact *that the dead statute fed and clothed many hundreds of thousands of people in this country. At that time he said the Prime Minister would not even give the people a stone or a serpent. In his speech on Tuesday he admitted that the Prime Minister now is giving them a stone and a serpent. Well, if the dead statute so far exceeded the expectations of the right hon. gentleman what may we not expect from the stone and the serpent?
There is one other point I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker. The right hon. gentleman complains that the Prime Minister has offered a stone and a serpent. I ask any member of this house or any electors throughout this country to read the speech delivered by the right hon. gentleman in 1930 and see if they can find out what he intends to give the people as a substitute.
One other thing struck me very forcibly in the remarks of my right hon. friend, as well as in those of the ex-M'inister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon. That hon. gentleman dealt at very great length with the constitutional question. Every word of that address and a great part of the address of the right hon. leader of the opposition, was predicated upon the assumption that, immediately this statute is passed, the people of this country are going to try to destroy it. It seems to me that the members of this house ought to represent pretty well the views of the people, and when every party is claiming the honour of having fathered this legislation it is a strange assumption to make that the people whom they represent are going to set out to destroy it. Why, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) were almost vying with each other as to who originated this scheme, and we have no fault to find with that. But it must seem strange to the people of this country that all parties in this House of Commons should vie

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. McIntosh
with each other in commending this legislation, in supporting the very principle behind it and declaring that if it is to be effective it must be national and not provincial. That is the one point upon which all are heartily agreed, and yet we are told that the people whose views hon. members of this house are supposed to represent are going to set out to destroy this measure. And it is not merely this particular measure, with any faults the opposition may think it has; if they destroy it they destroy the whole principle. If they attack its constitutionality they make the enactment of any statute of the kind utterly impossible. I do not believe the people of Canada will tolerate that attitude on the part of any political party or group. I believe they will insist that hon. members who have supported the measure, their followers and their lieutenants in the provinces, continue to take the same stand, namely that this legislation is for the benefit of the Canadian people, and I believe the Canadian people will not tolerate any attempt to destroy it.
This afternoon the ex-Minister of Justice made a very strong plea for the constitution. He said Canada had grown and developed but that the constitution had stood still. Every constitution in the world is subject to two dangers. One is the reckless and thoughtless disregard for the constitution. I do not believe any party in this chamber can be charged with that. I am sure all hon. members will agree that the constitution has never been endangered by the introduction of legislation for the masses of the people. The second danger, however, to which every constitution is subject is that of holding so rigidly to its letter and form that it becomes subversive of all measures for the amelioration of the wants and needs of the people. To my mind that is the greatest danger which can threaten any constitution. So long as it meets the needs of the people and brings relief where relief is required, the danger is not great, because there is a sufficient body of sound and sane opinion behind it. But the danger is very real when we hold to the letter and form to such an extent that the constitution becomes not a bulwark of the liberty of the people but simply an obstacle to all progress and all reforms tending to alleviate suffering. That I believe is the only real danger facing our constitution to-day. I should be interested to know who throughout the length and breadth of the land are so completely out of touch with the general sentiment in Canada-because either they or every hon. member in the house is out of 92582-53
