In the words of the poet, whither are our friends going? In the historic Conservative party of Great Britain the word "Conservative" was the most dominant. The party was supposed to be a Conservative party in opposition to the subversive policy of the Whigs. Then at a later time the Conservative party took on the name of the constructive and positive party with regard to constitutional reform as opposed to the radicalism of the Liberals. There is their basic history in a constitutional sense. In other words they were-and are still-the party of laissez-faire. They wanted to conserve and stand on the same platform politically forever and ever almost, while the Liberal party was ever going onward, making progress and putting through radical measures on behalf of the people.
In regard to the basic social and political policies of the Liberal party as the British party of parliamentary reform, all we need to know is that the Liberal party has always stood for a policy of peace, retrenchment and
lMr. McIntosh.]
reform. These principles have always been fundamental in the evolution of the party and they are as fundamental to-day as ever. The Liberal party has always stood for international peace and justice based on national honour and national self-respect. In a reform or retrenchment sense Liberals have ever stood for lowering government expenditures, cutting down the national debt and the national interest and lowering taxation. And the Liberal party stands by these policies yet.
In the way of constructive reform all one has to do is to read British history from 1800 to 1832 and onward through the times when Lord John Russell, Sir Robert Peel, Palmer-ton, Gladstone, and later Asquith and Lloyd George piloted the Liberal party in Great Britain. The Liberal party has continually stood for civil and religious liberty; for a belief in human personality; for a belief in the value of human energy; for the state creating conditions which would be more satisfactory for the average worker; for standing by the mastery of each individual's capacity, as well as for establishing a real policy of equality of opportunity. Down through the period of British history this policy of sound radicalism or sound reform on the part of the Liberal party was continued-right down to the war and subsequently. Liberal policy was at the back of practically every article of the treaty of peace. The Liberal party stood for fair and humane labour conditions for men, women and children abroad and in their own country; for the just treatment of the natives of territories under their control; for the supervision of the traffic in women and children; for the supervision of the traffic in opium and other dangerous drugs; for supervision of the traffic in arms and ammunition; for taking a stand on behalf of controlling international disease and ill health The physical and intellectual welfare of industrial workers in Great Britain and in the world was likewise espoused, and the necessity was urged for action on the fundamental causes of national and international unrest. That is why the Liberal party later gave all its support to the labour portions of the peace treaty and took the stand that labour should not be looked upon as a saleable commodity. Liberalism was constantly upholding the right of free association for employers and employees; a reasonable standard of living; the eight hour day and the forty-eight hour week, and a weekly day of rest. It stood further for equal remuneration for work done by men and women, and

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. McIntosh
for equality of treatment for all workers; for the rigid inspection of factories in which industrial employees were working.
The Liberal party in Canada has also a substantial policy in the way of peace because its plank in that regard is as follows:
The Liberal party will seek to further wherever possible those courses in international relations which make for peace and good will among nations, and promote friendly intercourse between them. It will seek to further the work of the League of Nations.

Let me discuss for a moment or two the industrial and international relations committee report presented to parliament on May 23, 1929. I wish to show the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite on this question of unemployment insurance. In presenting the report on that date I tried to indicate, as chairman of the committee, that the committee had done its best to obey the mandate of parliament to investigate and report upon this very intricate and technical question. In analyzing the report I went on to show that its adoption was vital inasmuch as it was in the direction of industrial and universal peace, which is based on international justice. I emphasized the importance of the report both nationally and internationally. It was pointed out that the question could not be dodged, that the time had come for action, and the report embodied the endorsation and the affirmation of the principle of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. It also supported the principle of a contributory system involving the employer, the state and the employee, and it went on to discuss a comprehensive national health policy as well as the securing of further data after the taking of the census. It proposed a conference between the provinces and the dominion in order to bring about the necessary cooperation without which this important problem could not be approached effectively.
When the committee's report came before parliament an amendment was moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and an important debate ensued on the question. The hon. gentleman expressed the opinion that the report should be referred back to the committee for reconsideration and further report and that there should be something more tangible, more concrete. He held that the report was really a step backward. The question of jurisdiction

The amendment itself was to the effect that the report should be sent back to the committee and that the provinces should be requested to pass the necessary legislation giving up their jurisdiction with a view to having the matter dealt with nationally. That gave rise to considerable debate in the house, and I think it is necessary to run through that debate in order to indicate the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite on this very important problem.
At page 2776 of Hansard of May 23, 1929, I find the following statement by the present Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) on this question. He quoted the amendment, which was:
That the said report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations be not now concurred in but that it be referred back to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations with instructions that they have power to amend the same by adding thereto a clause recommending that all the provinces of the dominion be requested to pass legislation under which the jurisdiction in relation to legislation providing for unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance, based on compulsory contribution and which is now claimed to be within or subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, be vested in the dominion government.
The hon. gentleman followed that up by saying:
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that, when specific jurisdiction is vested under the constitution in the provinces, the provinces by any conceivable legislation could' revest that jurisdiction in the dominion parliament? It seems to me to be the most extraordinary suggestion I have heard for some time.
That was the point of view of the Secretary of State on that occasion. But the hon. gentleman also made this statement:
That being admitted, why should the parliament of Canada express a gratuitous opinion upon a public matter which is not within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament or the administrative jurisdiction of the government responsible to parliament? Why should we in this parliament, who have very extended duties and obligations to the public, set ourselves up as the judges of the duties and responsibilities of members of the several legislatures, and attempt, by adopting a report of a nature which I have read, to superimpose our gratuitous opinions upon the legislatures of the provinces and the governments w'hich are responsible to those legislatures? Even if we adopt the report of the committee in its present form, we are going far outside of any jurisdiction committed to the parliament of Canada,

There we see the hon. gentleman, who is a member of the present ministry, taking the stand that it was an insult to the provinces, an insult to any provincial government in Canada, that even an opinion should be expressed at that time in the House of Commons on this question. Well, as I have said, it is a long distance between an attitude of that kind and the attitude which we have demonstrated on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite on the present occasion. Then the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens), then representing Vancouver Centre, made the statement that the report was all eyewash; that was his attitude. And a little further on at page 2787 we have the point of view of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) on the amendment which was before the house. These are his words:
While Bourinot's opinion was as Your Honour has quoted, nevertheless it is pointed out in May, as in the rules of the house, that when the matter is clearly a subject that this house should not pronounce upon, it should not be asked to do so, because by so doing the house would be pronouncing on something over which it has no jurisdiction. The last part of the amendment asks that the legislative powers-the legislative powers, mark you-of the provinces, which are defined by section 92 of the British North America Act, shall be vested in the dominion government.
In other words, the right hon. gentleman was of the opinion, that there should be no pronouncement whatsoever on the subject. His attitude was practically the same as the Secretary of State's, for that hon. gentleman said that no gratuitous opinion should be advanced on that report because it was purely a provincial problem.
On the other hand, we find that the attitude of the Liberal party on this question has been sound throughout; you will find it so in that very debate. The then Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) took the view that the matter was entirely one for the provinces; it came within the ambit of provincial jurisdiction. He cited the danger of interfering in a matter of this kind; there was no doubt in the minds of the law officers of the crown, nor was there any doubt about the constitution in that regard. My contention is that that point of view by Tory journalism all over Canada built up a menacing volume of public opinion at that time detrimental to insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. That opinion was emphasized in this house-as I have shown-excepting to the right of the Speaker, that is on the part of the government of the day. Such opinion had an adverse effect upon the provinces. There was a division of opinion on this important question all over Canada because of the attitude of the Journal, as shown by the attitude the provinces took in regard to it. At that time there was no volume of public opinion in favour of this question outside members of the Liberal party in the house and out of it. There is no doubt about that at all. The Conservative party was quite hostile to the question of social insurance in the house; they poured cold water on it every time they could; they never spoke a word in favour of it and they discounted it whenever the opportunity arose.
The report of the industrial and international relations committee was sent to the different provinces, and what do we find? We find that there was no cooperation shown by the provinces with regard to this report, consequently no action was possible in connection with the question of unemployment insurance in 1929. I have before me the report from Nova Scotia. At that time the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) was Prime Minister of that province and today he is in the ministry and is, I am told, whole-heartedly for unemployment insurance. What was his attitude in 1929? Did he say that his province favoured it? Did he say that his province would support it? Did he give any aid to the then Liberal government to evolve a policy that would later meet unemployment all over Canada? He never said a word in favour of it. This is the letter dated August 3, 1928, from Halifax:
Dear Sir:
I have your letter of July 31.
This is in answer to Mr. Heenan, then Minister of Labour, who sent out this report to all the provinces.
The whole subject matter will have to be studied with great care by the government, and for that purpose we will await the printed report of the minutes of proceedings and evidence.
fMr. McIntosh.]

E. N. Rhodes,
Premier.

Of course I recognize the desirability of some such provisions as these, but I think you will understand that, faced with the question of old age pensions and whait I regret to say seems to be the probable withdrawal by your government of the assistance to technical education, it is utterly impossible for a province with such limited means as New Brunswick to consider, at all, the subject about which you write. -we have 245 members claiming responsiblity for one child. Now, it can't be done. Many men have been mentioned in this house who have used the constitution as a barrier to progress, and the thought crossed my mind that it is a good thing there is not a constitutional Guy Fawkes around.
I think it is fair to say that governmental institutions in their fundamental concept should deal with the major risks of life from the viewpoint of the great majority that make up the working force of this and every other country. I think those major risks can be boiled down to three. One is sickness and the obligations arising out of sickness; another is unemployment, the worry, the trials and the tribulations of men and women who are anxious to work and unable to get the opportunity to earn a livelihood and provide for themselves and their dependents; and a third is the problem of old age and the fear of destitution. These are three fundamental problems in the life of the nation, simply stated; and since the dawn of history mankind has been wrestling with them. I think also one may safely say that we have moved very slowly towards their solution. In the material sphere enormous progress has been made in the last century, progress of a kind and on a scale unexcelled in the history of the w'orld. In fact we have almost invented ourselves out of a way to earn our livelihood. We have been so clever that we have forced millions of men and women on this continent to walk the streets owing to the introduction of the machine. I would like this to be considered by the government, that notwithstanding this legislation they are setting in motion, they should not lose sight of the great responsibility confronting them under present day conditions, concerning the problem that we almost forget about because of the depression, that of being too old at fifty-five to obtain gainful employment. That problem existed even in the most prosperous times. Then there is the problem of technological unemployment. The other day I
840	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mitchell
saw figures which have not been disputed, showing that even with the depression, if the productive forces of the United States were on the 1929 level, with the reduction of the working day to six hours they still would have an army of unemployed in that country numbering 6,000,000. You cannot wish yourself out of a jam like that. If private employers will not give leadership and adjust their business structures to meet the crying need for employment then in my judgment the duty lies with the government to provide that leadership. That is what I have always maintained. I think the test of any society, industrial or agricultural, is its ability to insure the membership of that society against the economic hazards of life, and I think that should be the pressing force behind the legislative functions of government. Security must be the cornerstone of any nation if progress is to be made. I think the test should and must be the degree of security given the individual in the form of productive employment and protection against such hazards as I have mentioned.
At the moment, Mr. Speaker, we are merely dealing with the [DOT] principle of the bill; we are not dealing with the sections. I think the principles boil down to two questions, is the bill constitutional, and shall we have contributory or non-contributory unemployment insurance. In the few remarks I make I am going to discuss the bill from that standpoint. This afternoon I listened to the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who discussed the constitutional aspect of the measure. He pointed out very clearly the clauses of the treaty of Versailles affecting the working-people of the nations engaged in the war. He pointed out the solemn obligations under that treaty of peace that pledged the nations to move in a certain direction in order to meet pressing problems as they affected the daily lives of the people in the respective countries at the close of the war. I was in the war; I was in England at the conclusion of the war, and I have a very vivid recollection of the cry of Lloyd George, "Make this a country fit for heroes to live in," and so on. I believe the men came back from the war with faith-almost a divine faith, I might say-that the promises contained in the peace treaty would be implemented by both the victorious and the defeated nations, but in this dominion it has taken fourteen years for us to carry out the promises incorporated in the treaty of Versailles.
So we have the constitutional question brought up in connection with this matter.
I know the opinion of the average working-fMr. Mitchell.]
man; I think I can reflect it as well as anyone in this House of Commons. I came from the workshop to this house, and when my constituents are through with me I will go back to-

speechtext: The workhouse.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
My hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) says I will go back to the workhouse, and there may be more truth than fiction in that statement. The average workingmen are not greatly interested in the constitutional question. They want to get something done; they are asking, "When do we eat?" The average man in the street is saying, "For God's sake give us an opportunity for productive labour, so that we can meet our obligations and look after our families without need of charity." That is the cry of the man in the street to those having leadership in this dominion.
We are accustomed to this constitutional argument; it has been the barrier that has stood in the way of most social reform. I had a great deal to do with the propaganda carried on in this country for the establishment of an old age pension scheme in Canada. I remember the way that proposal was bandied from one government to another; eventually, of course, we did get a system of old age pensions. Then I have a vivid recollection of the opposition to these schemes that have been advocated by labour for many years. I would like to ask these provinces to come out in the open and say so if they do not want a system of unemployment insurance. Let them be frank about it if they do not want these very necessary reforms that must be carried out if the problems of mass production and modern industry are to be met. I have not heard them; I do not think any member of this house has heard them make that statement. Let us be frank about it; let us come out and say so if we are opposed to these things. I object very strenuously to any man in this country mixing up the rights of minorities with the obvious necessity of moving in the direction in which this legislaton goes. There is no man in this house or in this country who is more fixed in his opinions as to the rights of minorities than I am, but I do not believe that the rights of minorities should be used as a smoke screen to prevent the passage of legislation of this description and its practical application in this country. If the contention of the hon. member for Quebec East is sound, this bill is not worth the paper it is written on. Let us be frank about it; let us tell the people of

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mitchell
Canada that if the constitutional position taken by the hon. member is sound, this House of Commons is wasting its time.
I know the western provinces do not care much about the constitutional aspect of it. Last year in this house I quoted a statement by the then Premier of Alberta, Hon. J. E. Brownlee, which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 21, 1934. Mr. Brownlee said that all the western provinces had agreed to give up their constitutional rights in order to make such legislation possible, and he said the dominion government was working on a measure along that line. That was in answer to a question by the executive board of the Alberta federation of labour, asking the government of that province to lend its aid to the institution of an unemployment insurance measure in that province.
I also think we should be very frank with the working people of this dominion, and disabuse their minds of the belief that this legislation can meet the problem of unemployment. I know that in the propaganda stage that precedes the launching of any legislation of this kind statements are apt to be made by enthusiasts that would lead people to believe more than is actually the case. That is a fact that one encounters in connection with all legislation, whether it be social or otherwise. Extravagant statements are made as to what can be done by legislation similar to this. I think it should be made clear that the government must initiate policies to take care of the tremendous unemployment problem in this dominion, and no attempt should be made to lead the people to believe that this legislation can be a solution for that problem. It should be made clear also that this does not relieve this government or any government of its duty to supply food and shelter for those who at the moment are on relief. That is a problem that must be meit until those unfortunate people are able again to take their part in the industrial or agricultural life of this dominion. Neither do I think it does us any good to say why someone else did not do this, what somebody said in 1896 or 1902. or whether somebody has changed his mind in the last two years. After all is said and done a man who cannot change his mind -well, he never had one. I am not interested only in a recital of the achievements of the group to which I belong, or to a discussion of the achievements of other political parties. I am most concerned about the passage of this legislation in the broadest possible form
and in terms through which the greatest number will derive benefit or advantage. It is a great tragedy that suffering has always been the midwife of progress. I believe it is fair to say that ten yeans ago no government in Canada would have taken the chance of passing legislation of this kind. Notwithstanding the fact that a large body of public opinion pressed for such legislation I do not believe opinion was strong enough to command the notice of any government. We have to be fair about it, and that is why I make that observation.
It would be easy for me to say that I have advocated this legislation for a lifetime, and in that way get some kudos out of it. It would be easy to say that hon. members in this comer of the house did so and so, but I believe we have to be perfectly frank about it. I question very much whether the average man or woman of ten years ago had any interest in unemployment insurance. At least that was my experience, and I believe if there had been any interest in the matter we would have an entirely different situation to-day. There would have been a scheme in force, broad in its application, one which would have lightened the mental strain and burden suffered because of the great depression.
We now come to a discussion of contributory and non-contributory unemployment insurance. Frankly, I believe in the contributory system, the system advocated by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and I make that choice without any equivocation. I hold the view that no nation which gives the people something for nothing can endure; we might as well be honest about it. Neither do I believe that the burden should fall too heavily upon the worker who comes under a scheme. It is my opinion that the present legislation goes too far in that direction, and that a greater burden should be placed on industry and on the government. We know that all social services, including even the salaries of hon. members in this chamber, are a charge on the living standards of the Canadian people, and any legislation involving an expenditure of money must in the final analysis have its effect on the productive forces and on the whole structure of the country. My greatest concern is that when the scheme is launched the workingman may have something to say about it. Unless a person helps to pay for a thing I question very much whether he has any right to say anything about its operation.
842	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Mitchell
One feature of the bill which meets with my approval is that the responsibility for administration is placed squarely where it belongs, namely upon the workers and employers in industry. Undoubtedly the workingmen have some right to say how the payments shall be made, how the operations of the act may be broadened, and generally to watch over its development. There can be no doubt that the scheme will have to be hammered out in the laboratory of the industrial structure of our country. We shall have to do the same as other nations have done, the same as Great Britain did, namely, work the scheme out by the process of trial and error; and quite possibly that work will not have been completed in this generation.
I appreciate the fact that to advocate a non-contributory system of unemployment insurance would be the most popular stand. I have no quarrel with people who hold that view; the right to agree is the basis of human freedom. After giving the matter very careful thought, however, I have some to doubt very much whether we could have a system of non-contributory unemployment insurance without having a dictatorship. We could not have that form of protection unless the state could say to the worker, "This is the amount you will be paid; this is the kind of work you will do"-and have control of all the movements of the individual connected with the scheme. We must remember that this is to a great extent an agricultural country, and any scheme must meet the views or be capable of receiving the support of that great body of people.

speechtext:
I shall tell you in a moment. That is why I believe a non-contributory scheme would be unsound. Someone has asked: What do they do in dictatorships? Well, my reply is that any man with a bayonet in his fist can be a dictator, so long as he does not stick it into himself. I believe that has been proved.
Frankly a non-contributory scheme would not, in my opinion, meet with the views of the average Canadian. The people in this country would rather help to administer and pay for their scheme. Believing that, undoubtedly I should take responsibility of saying so. In working out the scheme the government must take into consideration seasonal employment, and may I indicate in passing that the bill does not make provision for those who are working on a five day or even a four day week, a fault which can be

remedied when the bill reaches the committee. Further, consideration must be given to the fact that many people engaged in industry are working on short time. Arrangements should be made whereby those people can meet the payments without any undue hardship on themselves, and the legislation must be elastic enough to permit the admission of such people. No man should be penalized or placed outside the scope of the legislation because of circumstances over which he has no control. Many men, particularly in the railroad industry, who would ordinarily be engaged in steady labour are working, due to the depression, only two weeks a month.
The measure contains the further constructive suggestion, namely that it will make use of the employment agencies, or as they are called in Great Britain, the labour exchanges. It will permit the mobilization and organization of labour on a much more satisfactory scale than has obtained before in Canada. To those who speak of provincial schemes I would point out the utter impracticability of a provincial scheme in legislation of this kind. A man might live in Ontario, for example, and the scheme might not be in existence in Quebec or Manitoba. That man would be frozen to working in Ontario in order to gain the benefits of the insurance scheme. Anyone who has made any study at all of labour matters knows that you should not deny the worker the right to go from one end of this dominion to the other, should the need arise, in search of employment. If you had a provincial scheme you can readily see how the worker would lose the benefits of it-unless he went into the province in which the legislation was operating. We have seen that in practical application so far as the old age pension scheme is concerned. Notwithstanding the fact that that legislation has been in existence since 1927, there are still three or four provinces, Quebec for example, which have not brought that scheme into being. In connection with mothers' allowances we saw how a widow living outside the boundaries of a province where mothers' allowances were in effect would immediately move into Ontario, for instance, to qualify under the residence rule for the allowance under the act. So we have had practical experience of the unsoundness of attempting to deal with these great social problems on a purely provincial basis. I think that has been proven conclusively, and in my judgment we would be foolish-I do not say that in any critical sense-if we did not take cognizance of the very practical experience we have had in the application of measures of this kind.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Ralston
When the bill gets into the committee stage I shall have a great deal to say in connection with incidentals surrounding the application of particular clauses of the bill itself. I have often said that men are the instruments of policy, and one of the most important factors in the successful application of legislation of this kind is that those in charge of its administration shall be sympathetic to the legislation. That is a very important feature that must be borne in mind by the government, that men in charge of applying this form of legislation should be sincere and sympathetic in the broadest sense, so that the law may have as wide an application as possible in the shortest possible time. So, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the government will use good judgment in selecting men who have had some practical experience in the problems of the labour men of this country, and that on the other hand they will select men who are imbued with the soundness of enactments of this character and have a vision of its possibilities for good in the lives of the working men and women of this dominion.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this is a forward step, and I would be insincere if I did not say so. There are many criticisms one could offer of the measure, but I am now endorsing the principle of the bill because it is a form of legislation that meets a crying need in any industrial country. It must be remembered that even in the midst of this depression there are tens of thousands of borderline cases who should be on relief and whom a measure of this kind will help tremendously. When the scheme gets into its stride, if we ever get out of this depression, I visualize a constructive approach to the problem of ironing out the inequalities of seasonal occupation in this country. There are also potentialities in the stabilization of working conditions and of maintaining the demand for consumption on the part of the Canadian people, the benefits of which will be reflected back to agriculture. That has been proven in other countries. In Great Britain at the moment one sees tremendous sums of money in circulation through schemes of this kind and which, under the conditions under which we are living at the moment, would otherwise be tied up in the banks and in strong boxes throughout the country.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am going to support the principle of the bill and ask for its widest application for the benefit of the working people of this dominion.

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I think perhaps a word or two should be said with regard to some phases of the matter
which have been covered to some extent but which might deserve a little more amplification.
In the first place let me say to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Mitchell) that I rise to support and we on this side of the house will support in principle the idea of unemployment insurance. It is not any new feature as far as those on this side of the house are concerned. It is a matter which has engaged the attention of members of this side of the house for a number of years, as has been indicated by the record which has been placed on Hansard by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe); and regardless of the fact that my hon. friend is not interested in the history of the activities of the other parties in connection with this measure, it seems to me that it is a matter of some interest to the country generally to know whether or not this measure is being brought forward at the present time by those who have consistently in season and out of season supported the principle, or whether it is being brought forward, just on the eve of an election, in the form of a so-called reform program in entire contradiction of the position which has been taken by the right hon. leader of the government and his colleagues almost right up to the time he gave his radio broadcasts.
I want to say to my hon. friend who has just sat down, and to you, Mr. Speaker, that the record of the Liberal party has been a steady effort towards putting on the statute books a comprehensive, workable and valid unemployment insurance measure. That record is indicated by the fact that it was the Liberal party which in 1926, and again in 1927, advanced the principle of old age pensions, and after their old age pension measure was defeated by the Conservative majority in another place succeeded in putting it upon the statute books where to-day its benefits are being enjoyed by the old people of this country almost from one end to the other. This it seems to me is a matter which the people of this country will take into consideration when they are considering the sincerity of those who are supporting the bill at the present time.
May I say further that my right hon. leader made a declaration in this house, not on the eve of an election, but over two years ago, indicating that the Liberal party had as a plank in their platform a national unemployment insurance measure, and the steps which had
844	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Ralston
been taken and were being taken to carry that out are well known to members of this house and this country.
When I mention my leader I want to say this, that the members of this party take some satisfaction in the fact that the leader of the Liberal party has in season and out of season during his whole life been interested in social legislation-not at the last minute, just on the eve of an election in 1935, but year after year his whole training, his experience and his activities have been in the direction of social reform. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I think we can say with considerable pride that the record of the leader of the Liberal party is not excelled at least by any statesman living or dead in Canada for his attention to and interest in matters that pertain to the social welfare of the people of this country. The other night there was put on Hansard the record of the Liberal party in connection with social legislation. It went back to the days of the establishment of the Department of Labour, which was followed by the passing of the conciliation act; with the passing of the railways dispute act; the passing of fair wages provisions, whereby employees of the dominion government received the benefit of the fair wages statute and of the eight hour day; the passing of the Combines Investigation Act; the passing of the Technical Education Act of 1919, which was the outcome of a commission that had been appointed by the leader of the opposition when he was in power; and with the passing of the Old Age Pensions Act. That is a record in which the Liberal party takes some pride, and therefore it comes as a natural step that the members of the Liberal party should support an unemployment insurance measure. But the members of that party take as much pride in the fact that its leader has not only worked through practical legislation but has devoted his life to the education of the people of this dominion and the spreading of information among them in connection with measures along this line; and I am not at all sure that the foundations of the legislation which we are dealing with to-night and of previous legislation of this kind cannot be found in the fact that the people of Canada have been informed and have had their minds concentrated upon such measures through the efforts of the present leader of the opposition and former Prime Minister of Canada.
Let me emphasize what I said a minute ago, that the peculiar satisfaction which we have on this side of the house is that the views which the leader of the opposition represents

here as leader of the Liberal party are convictions which are inherent in every fibre of his being and which he has practised from the time he entered public life, and are not the result of an overnight change of coat such as took place early this year when the Prime Minister felt the dread of the wintry blasts of the condemnation of the people at the polls. My right hon. friend is able to change legal opinions as he is able to change other views in connection with his public life. It is typical of him. My hon. friend who has just spoken says that it is no discredit to a man to change his mind. That may be so, but at the same time we Should expect some constancy in public men.

I know that my hon. friends have been taught not to expect that on their side of the house. The Prime Minister is the gentleman who not long ago in this house was talking about sound money and deprecating the idea of turning on the printing press, and yet he is the very gentleman who suddenly was found, only a short time afterwards, doing a sleight of hand inflation trick-I use that term in no invidious sense-by means first of becoming a borrower from the banks, issuing treasury notes, and the next moment becoming a lender to the banks, printing about $35,000,000 of paper currency to loan against the treasury notes he had just issued. That is the gentleman who had talked about sound money. We have had in the last six months the same gentleman who talked about sound money issuing currency to the extent of between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000, carrying it to the banks and issuing cheques, notwithstanding the fact that the gold reserve has not increased; and yet he was extremely wrathy, particularly at those in one corner of the house, who talked about the possibilities of turning on the printing press. The same gentleman, two or three years ago, when the matter of a central bank came up, stood in his place and intimated that there was no need whatever of a central bank, that the Finance Act contained all the provisions necessary for the financial operations of the country; and though he did not use the word "ridiculous" he intimated that it was ridiculous to talk of a central bank in this country. And yet we find that on January 2 or 3, I forget which broadcast it was, he was boasting of the fact that his reform program had commenced and that he had inaugurated a central bank, the very thing he had opposed

I have stated exactly what he did. On the motion of an hon. member on this side of the house he intimated that the Finance Act would probably do this country, I think he said, for a period of fifty years, so far as he knew. But the central bank was suddenly grasped as one of the measures of reform; and as a matter of fact he did not know it was a reform when he put it on the statute books, but only realized it on the first of January this year.
And then we find him dealing with social reforms. He is not one who has extreme familiarity with matters of social legislation. Only a year ago he was speaking in Toronto and he had not very much idea of these social reform measures, these social reform activities and this social reform program. He said:
I would like to promise you a spectacular move that would make you hip, hip. hurrah; but, gentlemen, you did too much of that a few years ago, forgetting that some day the bills would have to be paid. We cannot offer you anything spectacular-nothing but thrift and hard work.
That was only February 2, 1934. He did not intimate that any reform program was necessary, but a little later in the year he said:
I believe we have passed and left behind us the great depression we encountered in 1929 and 1930. We are standing on the threshhold of a greater progress and greater prosperity than we have ever known.
That was June 8, 1934, and on August 27 he spoke at Quebec of the depression "of late lamented memory." Then on the first of October in London he spoke of "the steady progress which Canada has made in the last eighteen months." And on the very day that the newspapers published the report of his radio speech there appeared an advertisement issued by his government through the Department of Trade and Commerce:
As the year 1934 passes into history, Canada can look back on a period of unimpaired progress so definitely sustained that it has brought us to the pathway that leads to sound, sensible and stable prosperity.
That was on January 1, and yet on January 2 my right hon. friend said over the radio:
The world is in tragic circumstances. The signs of recovery are few and doubtful; the signs of trouble are many and they do not lessen. The world is searching pathetically for safety and prosperity. It will find them only when each nation, resolute to effect its own regeneration, will come to a meeting place with all the others in the spirit which declares that even the most powerful among them has no real economic independence of the rest. That time has not yet come. Meanwhile dangers abound.
And a few lines further down he said:
But the facts, grave as they are, do not cast me down nor will they you. I am deeply anxious, but I can never doubt this country's coming triumph if you will range yourselves on the side of progress and reform. For then we will fight on, you and I, and we will win.
Then, although Canada was according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the way to sound and sensible prosperity, on the next page there appeared this:
Reform or no reform! I raise that issue squarely. I nail the flag of progress to the masthead. I summon the power of the state to its support.
That was stated by the gentleman who a year before had said, "We have nothing spectacular to offer, nothing but thrift and hard work." Now my right hon. friend has indicated to us what the trouble really was. He said in that same broadcast speech-and
1	am paraphrasing him now-"I had people coming to me asking me to put reform measures upon the statute books." Then he goes on:
I can assure you that it was not easy to say no. I had to harden my heart. I did so, but with more sorrow and sadness than I have ever known in my life before. I can assure you with equal truth that, had we said yes to those sometimes frantic pleas, Canada would not have been where it is to-day. We had to defer reform until the time for reform had come.
The time for reform came just on January
2	in the year of the election when the last
session of parliament was about to be convened. What a thrill this has given our hon. friends! Some of them have said: He has turned socialist. Others said that he had turned radical.	People said that he had
turned reformer. I think the country knew what had happened-nothing more than that he had electionitis. We know, as we have reason to know, remembering the campaign of 1930, that when he is suffering from that fever he is liable to say almost anything. After all, in the bill that we have before us to-night, is it really a policy of reform which my right hon. friend is bringing before the country or is it a policy of "recant"? I presume my right hon. friend, if I am to

In his address the other
day in introducing the resolution he referred to the jurisdiction, but nothing whatever was said about the fact that he himself, eminent lawyer as he is, had no longer ago than September last indicated to the provinces that, at least in his opinion and speaking as Prime Minister of Canada, they had exclusive jurisdiction. Already, if we are to judge by the bill which is before us, the exaggerations of the reform program are plainly evident. Unemployment insurance was one of the high lights of that program, and what have we before us? We have a bill which purports to provide for unemployment insurance. The Prime Minister has quite frankly and sincerely said that it is not a recovery measure. It is not an emergency measure; it is not a relief measure; it is something which will not take effect for some time. My hon. friend who spoke last said: When will it take effect? We know a man has to contribute for at least forty weeks before he gets any benefit at all, so it means that for at least a year nobody in this country will receive any benefits from this legislation.
But leaving out the question of delay, what else have we? We have a bill which omits to make any provision whatever for those engaged in three out of the four primary industries in this dominion, although they are to be taxed to pay for the others. That is the first thing with regard to the bill. The second is that it is a bill which, as I said a moment ago, admittedly does nothing whatever to deal with the present situation. Third -and I wish I could put this in as graphic language as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) did the other night-one of the features of the bill which I think the government will surely see ought to be changed is that which appears to emphasize and glorify the bureaucratic type of government which is exemplified in other countries

by the exhaustion of the alphabet in connection with the different boards, committees and commissions they have there. This bill piles commissions on committees and boards on commission in addition to referees and umpires. It adds to the burdens of the taxpayers and to the irritation of those who come under the provisions of the measure. It seems to me a pretty definite attempt by the government to honeycomb our national life with a group of, so far as parliament is concerned, irresponsible and detached bodies who function independently of any departmental responsibility and who go to make officialdom the master rather than the servant of the people of this country. Fourthly, this bill which was one of the high lights of the Prime Minister's reform program, relies for its very foundation upon the shifting sands of questionable legal validity. As I go on, I want to call to witness the Prime Minister himself, his Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and his Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) in support of that statement.
The radio speech is now under the microscope. Let us compare this bill with that radio speech. The flag of progress has not been nailed very high on the mast so far as this bill is concerned.

speechtext:
Seventeen other countries have unemployment insurance. This matter is nothing new, nothing novel. My right hon. friend has not apparently gone very far along the line of reform in this the first bill which he has brought down to implement his reform program. But I am going to leave aside the matter of the scope of the measure and the question of the machinery provided in it and to deal for just a moment or two with what it seems to me is the first essential of any bill and what will be an important consideration for anybody who has to do w'ith this measure and who expects to get any benefit from it, namely, the question of its validity. The bill will not be of very much good if, as my hon. friend who spoke before me said, it is unenforceable. As he said, in that case it is just a piece of waste paper and we are wasting our time. Under this legislation certain rights to benefits are conferred, and that is the important matter so far as the working people of this country are concerned. In addition to that and supporting it is the obligation of the employer to pay. That is imposed by the bill. In addition to that there is the obligation of the employee to pay. That is imposed by the bill. In addition to that there is a provision which gives the employer

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Ralston
authority to collect from the employee the assessment as set forth in the bill. These are matters regarded as property and civil rights and within the jurisdiction of the provinces. If the contributions cannot be enforced or if a contribution by the central body to the beneficiary cannot be enforced, the legislation is an empty shell and a mockery.
I am not going to deal with the legal point, that is to discuss the radio case, the aeronautics case, the Snider case and others referred to by the Prime Minister at some length. I want to say just this: There has been prior to the time he introduced this bill a universal admission that such a measure was not within the legislative competence of this parliament. Until my right hon. friend spoke the other day when he introduced the resolution, neither he nor any of his ministers ever expressed any opinion other than that which was expressed by him in September last when he wrote to the provinces. Under these circumstances the situation is rather grave. My right hon. friend ought to give a fuller explanation than he has done with regard to what he considers to be the fundamentals upon which the validity of this bill can be supported. He is not an inexperienced counsel; he is a most experienced one; he has had experience in the privy council in constitutional cases; and when a man of his standing at the bar, a former president of the Canadian Bar Association, expresses an opinion on a legal matter, it is to be taken with a good deal of weight; and he has expressed this opinion in the house more than once on previous occasions. But we are left in the dark- except as far as my right hon. friend mentions treaty provisions-we are left in the dark as to the reason for the fundamental change that has taken place in his opinion and in the opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie)

who by the way has not favoured us with any address at all or any explanation on this rather important point as to the validity of the bill. Well, we have the preamble, and as was referred to by my friend the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) the preamble purports to support this legislation on the ground that it falls within article 23 and article 427 of the treaty of Versailles. The hon. member for Quebec East mentioned article 23 this afternoon and put part of it on record. The first part of article 23 indicates in the clearest terms that the whole undertaking, whatever the undertaking may be in that article, is:
Subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon. . . .
Where is the international convention in connection with this subject? Has it been agreed upon by this parliament? It has not. It has not even been brought down. Yet article 23 is being relied on by the Prime Minister as having created an obligation whereby section 132 of the British North America Act comes into play and whereby this parliament is given jurisdiction to enact legislation to carry out that obligation. But we must first have the obligation, and quite apart from the rather important introductory words I have quoted is there any definite obligation regarding unemployment insurance in the body of the article? As my hon. friend from Quebec East pointed out, I should think the only possible clause which might include unemployment insurance is to be found, if found at all, in the general words of subsection (a):
(a) will endeavour to secure and maintain fair and humane conditions of labour for men, women, and children, both in their own countries and in all countries to which their commercial and industrial relations extend, and for that purpose will establish and maintain the necessary international organizations.
Those are pretty general terms. To found jurisdiction in a field which is as competitive as that of provincial and dominion legislation it would seem to me that we ought to have more specific words than are there in order to establish that an unemployment insurance act is intra vires of this parliament. That is quite outside the first point I make, which is that whatever undertaking there is must be subject to and in accordance with-note those words particularly-an international convention, and such international convention has never been approved by this house or agreed to by Canada.
Then the other article invoked is 427. Well, that is even more nebulous. With all respect to those who drafted the treaty and to those who signed it, that article merely expresses a pious hope.
The high contracting parties, recognizing that the well being, physical, moral and intellectual, of industrial wage-earners is of supreme international importance, have framed, in order to further this great end', the permanent machinery provided for in section I and associated with that of the League of Nations.
They recognize-
No obligation yet.
-that differences of climate, habits and customs, of economic opportunity and industrial tradition, -make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment. But, holding as they do, that labour should not be regarded merely as an article of commerce, they think that there are methods and principles for regulating labour

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Ralston
conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
Among these methods and principles, the following seem to the high contracting parties to be of special and urgent importance:
And then they go on to enumerate a number of principles not one of which would seem to touch unemployment insurance. Now it does not require a lawyer to appreciate-the veriest layman can realize it, reading that- that there is no obligation contained in article 427. Yet we have gone to the trouble of reciting that as containing an obligation which entitles us to invoke section 132 of the British North America Act and gives us jurisdiction to enact this legislation.
The other provision referred to is the peace, order and good government provision of section 91, which was dealt with in the Snider case to which my right hon. friend referred, in which it was laid down that you could not invoke the general residuary powers contained in the words "peace, order and good government" in connection with any matter that fell strictly within the express subjects referred to in section 92. Property and civil rights are contained in section 92, therefore it would seem as if peace, order and good government would not be sufficient ground on which to base the validity of this legislation.
My right hon. friend has invoked an entirely new' principle. I suppose he says he has the authority of the judicial committee of the privy council for it. The judicial committee did, as my hon. friend from Quebec East said, in the aeronautics case and again in the radio case intimate that there was jurisdiction to carry out a treaty. But in those cases there was a treaty, as my hon. friend from Quebec East said-a binding treaty in each case. Here there is no treaty, not even a committal. Assuming there were some kind of a treaty, I am not sure that my right hon. friend is quite justified in going the length of assuming that Canada can enter into any treaty obligation at all, no matter how far it invades provincial jurisdiction, and still legislate to carry out that treaty under section 132. Let me give an instance. It will be said that it is farnfetched, but my right hon. friend's reasoning has to carry him that far. I have said that property and civil rights are within the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces. Public lands are within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and employment of labour is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Let us assume that the Dominion of Canada saw fit to make a treaty with Siam, under which Siam would agree to admit our
TMr. Ralston.]
fish free of duty-I am sure the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) will agree that that is highly desirable.

My right hon. friend in his statement the other day intimated that he thought it went that far. He said, as reported at page 643 of Hansard:
The ratio decidendi of the case is that section 132 confers on this parliament the power to discharge every obligation under a treaty, whether it affects the dominion or a province, which we enter into as part of the British empire. It may therefore be taken that wherever, as a part of the empire, a treaty is made by the parliament of Canada, this parliament has complete jurisdiction to deal with every phase of the subject matter of the treaty to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the provinces of confederation.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Ralston
1 point out that in this case of unemployment insurance there is no convention; what is his opinion therefore in this case? The Prime Minister says that the minister believes that in this case, notwithstanding that there is no convention, there is a binding obligation on the Dominion of Canada. I leave my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to deal with that himself if he cares to. I submit that there is no obligation under article 427 and no obligation under article 23, and there is no convention. I submit to my right hon. friend that there is the most serious doubt as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to pass this bill.
Then I go one step further. Leaving all these legal considerations aside we have the declaration of the Minister of Justice who is the attorney general of the dominion, in 1933, which was put on record this afternoon by my hon. friend from Quebec East. That was after the radio and aeronautics cases had been decided, and yet my hon. friend was still asserting that it was the provinces which had jurisdiction over unemployment insurance. In 1932, again after the radio and aeronautics cases had been decided, my right hon. friend said this was within the jurisdiction of the provinces. That citation was put on reicord, from Hansard 1932-33, page 1452, the other night by my right hon. leader. Then we have the words uttered in 1929 by the Secretary of State, to be found in Hansard for that year at page 2776, which were put on record by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), indicating the same view. When we have that situation do not my hon. friends, and particularly those interested in labour, think the proper thing to do in the first place would be to bring down the opinions of the law officers of the crown, in order to let this parliament see whether there is a possibility of this legislation really being good? Then do they not think, in the second place, that this matter should be submitted immediately to the Supreme Court of Canada in order that we may know whether we are going to enact legislation which, to use the expression of my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell), will be worth anything at all? In that connection I should like to cite what the Prime Minister said in connection with old age pensions. I quote from Hansard for 1926, at page 1970.
Faulty legislation placed upon the statute books the effect of which is to bring about chaos is very much to be deprecated. Anyone who has followed the course of legislation in any country, especially legislation of this character, will realize that where you rely solely and entirely upon experiments you have nothing 92582-54
but political action following political action and what was intended to be a great benefit has in many instances been a positive disadvantage to the very class it was intended to benefit.
Let me also remind my right hon. friend of what he said in a letter written to his former colleague, the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), as contained in sessional paper No. 99:
In due course a committee of eleven was appointed and you were elected chairman. From that time the committee had an absolutely free hand and no effort of any kind, shape or form was made to in any way limit or restrict its activities except that on more than one occasion we pointed' out to you the danger of creating in the minds of those interested. especially in the retail business, the impression that parliament could provide a remedy for the conditions of which they complained in view of the decisions of the courts as to the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures over contracts and price fixing.
I am pointing out the danger of creating in the minds of the people of the Dominion of Canada the impression that this parliament has the undoubted right to legislate in connection with the matter of unemployment insurance, in view of the legal position, and in view of the statements of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Secretary of State. I say that even if this measure is only for the future; even though it will not take effect until next year, so far as practical benefits are concerned, we ought to set ourselves to do a workmanlike job in connection with it. If the Prime Minister fails to do that I submit that it will corroborate and seal the conviction in the public mind that this legislation will prove to be not a benefit but rather a gold brick and a sham, as being inadequate in its provision in that, as I said a moment ago, it omits three of the primary industries entirely and secondly in that it establishes a bureaucracy. Thirdly, and worst of all, it is a measure born not of lifelong convictions and practical activities in connection with social legislation but bom of a feeling of desperation, and a knowledge on the part of the Prime Minister that he is about to face the electors of the dominion, and that he must look for something with which to obscure the promises he made in 1930.
I say to the right hon. gentleman that we will do all we can to assist in making this legislation, the sincerity of which we are bound to doubt, just as workable as possible, but at the same time we warn the people of Canada, just as he warned his Minister of Trade and Commerce, that we see the danger of a false impression being created in the minds of the

Mr. Speaker, before the debate closes I feel bound to express my disagreement with practically the whole house in regard to this measure. I am brought to my feet by reason of an observation made by my good friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) when he stated, somewhat mistakenly, that there were 245 fathers to this bill. I disclaim all paternity.
I am not going to develop my reasons for that statement, because it would be unfair to the house and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to prolong the debate unduly. I am opposed to this measure for many reasons. First, I am opposed to it bceause of the constitutional aspect which has been so ably presented by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and just now by the hon member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). For the life of me, I cannot understand how a single Liberal can vote for this measure after those three speeches. Second, l am opposed to it because it offers no cure whatever for the present unemployment situation, and this was handsomely admitted by the Prime Minister in introducing this measure. Third, I am opposed to it because it offers no relief in the future for a very large class of workers in some of the most important and permanent industries of the country, as was well pointed out by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth this evening. Fourth, because of conditions peculiar to this country such as the climate, the variety of occupations and the seasonal work, it is no remedy to copy a measure suitable to a country like Great Britain in order to cure an evil which with us is different and always will be different. I see in that another form of that old colonial spirit which thought that by copying anything on the statute books of England we were answering the needs of the people of Canada.
My fifth reason for opposing the measure is that it adds again to the load which is already weighing so heavily upon the shoulders of the ratepayers of this country; and when I speak of ratepayers I do not mean the wealthy ratepayers; I am speaking of that undefined class of small proprietors in the large centres, in the towns, in the villages, and a very large

number of farmers, who are already overloaded with taxes for schools and for the support of municipalities, provinces and the dominion, and who cannot bear any more taxation.
My sixth reason for being opposed to this legislation is that I find in it what I have seen growing in the last four or five years, and what evidently is going to continue to grow, whether the present government remains in power or whether my good friends here, the Liberals, come back to power. I refer to the tendency to purchase the good will of the various classes of the community by pouring public money into their pockets, favouring one class at the expense of a second, and a third class at the expense of a fourth. I have denounced it when it was a policy of high protection for industry; I denounce it now, because the effect of our whole so called social legislation is to debase the social spirit of our people, to create a fast growing class of beggars, loafers and crooked men, who expect the state to give them a living and who are endeavouring to avoid any individual or corporate effort to help save their own situation.
I am not going to deal at length with this or any other aspect of the problem. May I say that I have liberated my mind on this occasion and I may have further occasion to do it on other measures which will be presented to us. As a Canadian and as a friend of all classes in Canada, I believe we are on the wrong track towards remedying the evils that are upon us. No legislation, and especially no amount of money, will accomplish any good until we have created in the minds and hearts of all classes of Canadians a true social spirit. My good friend from East Hamilton knows about the experience in England in connection with this or similar legislation. Let me quote to him the opinion of a man who has given all his life to the welfare of the labouring class in England, a man whom I had the pleasure of knowing a good many years ago, a man who was then at the height of his popularity; I refer to John Burns. In the month of June, 1901, I met him in the city of London, after he had returned from a trip through Canada and the United States. I asked him to give me in a nutshell his impression of the labouring class in America as compared with the labourers of England. He said, in substance: "I will tell you frankly that the main difference I have found was this: The average American thinks of himself first and of his class after. We have been able to create a social spirit and bring about social legislation in England because

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
we have educated the English working man to think of his class first and himself afterwards." When he spoke of the average American he was including the Canadian along with the workingman of the United States. Ho said that of course he knew if the conditions of his class were improved he and his family would receive the benefits.
After forty years of experience in public life, having acquired knowledge of what is going on in different countries, I state quite frankly that the chief characteristic of our so-called American civilization, of our so-called high standard of life, is selfishness, individual selfishness, class selfishness. Almost every farmer thinks first of himself and then of the other farmers. Almost every workingman thinks first of himself and afterwards about his fellow workers. Every class of workmen think first of themselves and of their special trade; they do not care what will become of the workers in other unions or in other trades-and likewise with the industrialists and the professional men. Of course, that is an evil common to all new countries, the individuals of which migrated from various other countries. They come to the new country for the purpose of improving their individual conditions. Their main concern was and is the acquisition of individual wealth. Then came the days of corporations which each individual joins to get as much as he can from or through that corporation, as much as he can from the public treasury and from the consumers in the country. That is the social spirit we have. If we wish to have social legislation which will accomplish good, we must first work out and make firm the social spirit of the nation. We must imbue the labourer, the farmer, the business man and the professional man with the idea that if he wants to get something from the state and something from his fellow citizens, he must be prepared to give himself, his family and his country the full benefit of his effort to ameliorate his own condition and the condition of his class, and to help remedy the conditions of his country.
The policy of spoon feeding which has developed since the war is to my mind an instrument of debasement of public virility and social spirit. Our farmers to-day in the old province of Quebec are fast losing their sense of honour and their sense of duty. Many farmers to-day are thinking of going into bankruptcy and following the example which has been set by so many industrialists and merchants, namely that of cheating their creditors as much as they can, and then getting money from the state to make good. What
will they reap from going into fraudulent bankruptcy? That is the object many farmers have to-day. I have had experience with labour unions, and I have seldom found a true apostle of the proper social spirit among the labourers. At times, in the city of Montreal, I have been called upon to act as a friendly arbiter between groups of labourers and their employers. What did I find? On the one hand I found the employer thinking only of one thing, namely imposing the hardest conditions he could on his men, and on the other hand I found the men thinking of only one thing, namely, wresting from the company all they could, with entire disregard for the good of the community.
I have spoken at greater length than I had intended, but so far as I am concerned, if this goes to a vote, I shall record my vote against the second reading of the bill.

At the same time, however, since the introduction of the bill I have listened to the speeches of hon. members opposite and from time to time I have jotted down on a sheet of paper some of the illogical arguments they have used.
