According to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, apparently it is a greater crime to say that errors need correction and to have the vision and the courage to correct them than it is to be absolutely strict, as his leader has been, in putting into books, putting into speeches, putting into charts, putting into platforms and putting into the mouths of committees principles up to which he never lives.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou-rassa) who has just taken his seat, put his finger upon the truth when he said-I may not be using his exact words, but I believe I express his view

that if hon. gentlemen opposite who have spoken had any honesty in them they could not possibly support a measure which they have opposed ever since it was introduced. The hon. member for Labelle has been honest enough to say that he is going to oppose the measure; only a few moments ago he made that statement quite
852	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
frankly. He says he will not vote for the measure because he does not believe in it, as is obvious from his observations. Hon. members opposite do not believe in it. But, not believing, not one is going to be honest enough to vote against it. They are claiming that it is unconstitutional, claiming that it is inconsistent, claiming that the right hon. leader of the government is no fit leader for this country because he has changed his mind in one or two matters. Yet, claiming all that, they will vote for the measure. When we come to a vote on the second reading or third reading not one man of the whole group on the other side of the house, with the exception of the hon. member for Labelle, will have the courage to stand up and vote against it.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth stated a few moments ago that the trouble with the Prime Minister was that he had electionitis, simply because he saw the need for reform. May I ask the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth if his right hon. leader had electionitis when in the last session of parliament-in fact I believe it was after the last session of parliament and before the last election-he was responsible for passing orders in council making legal the eight hour day, and only the eight hour day, on public works in Canada, and yet did not put it into effect? Did his leader have electionitis, when just 'before the last election he took out of the treasury of the countiy tens of thousands of dollars-I do not remember the exact amount-and handed it in extra payment to the charwomen, forsooth, of the city of Ottawa, just before the election, ini order to make sure of their votes? There is no doubt about the purpose of that move.
Was his leader suffering from electionitis when he travelled from the Atlantic to the Pacific and talked of Senate reform, and then never touched it in nine years when he got back into power? Was his leader and the former Minister of Labour, a colleague of my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, suffering from electionitis when they travelled around this country and said, "We must have unemployment insurance in this country," and yet never did anything to put it into effect? The right hon. leader of the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth has done nothing in this house but talk of the principles which he upholds, yet did nothing to put those principles into practice when he had the power; and I say here that when the time comes the people of this country will have to judge between a man who always talks principles and does not practise them,
[,Mr. Manion.]
and a man like the present leader of the government, who may at times perhaps be inconsistent in some of his statements, but who has the courage and vision to bring into effect corrections of the economic system under which we- are living in order to save that system in which we believe. The whole boast of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and the other side of the house about their leader is that he has been consistent and my leader inconsistent. Somebody much greater than I once said that consistency was the bane of little minds, and I think that is probably true. I would point out that one of the names in English history which has come down to us during the last half century has been that of Sir Robert Peel, one of the greatest leaders that England ever produced, one of the greatest men that ever stood in the British parliament, and1 yet a man of whom it was said that 'before he finally went out of power he had put into effect practically everything that he had opposed earlier in his career. Is it then a crime to change one's ideas if one sees the need of change? I think it was Abraham Lincoln who said that anyone was welcome to his cast-off ideas; and my hon. friends opposite are welcome to the cast-off ideas of the present Prime Minister, or of any member on this side of the house.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, the hon. member for Quebec East, the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, and even the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) to-night in that masterly and classical manner of his, have been spending hours in this house telling the people of our country that this legislation that is proposed by the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. Well, if they are convinced that it is unconstitutional, and that it cannot be1 carried out, as they say- that the provinces will prevent its being carried out-should they not honestly and squarely oppose the measure instead of doing as they are doing, expressing their opposition to it in speech but pretending that they are going to support it in action? That is the attitude they are taking. They tell us that they are for this measure. Without exception hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house, one after the other, except the hon. merhber for Labelle, have stood up and said: I want it distinctly understood that I am for this measure, but I want it also distinctly understood that the measure is no good, it is unconstitutional. And anybody who has the sense of an ordinary workingman cannot help

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
but realize that they will do everything they can to make it unworkable if they ever get a chance to put it into effect The leader of the opposition the other day, in that two-hour weary and dreary speech of his, as usual, made the statement that his government could not put such a measure into effect because they had to balance the budget. Then he showed that they had balanced the budget, that between 1925 and 1930, he said, they had actually cut down the debt of this country by $240,000,000. That was the statement also made on a number of occasions by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, that they had cut down the debt of this country by $240,000,000. Well, if they were able to cut down the debt of this country by $240,000,000, were they not then in a position to do a little towards putting into force some of this social legislation that we are attempting to bring in, and was not that the proper time to put social legislation into effect, preparing for days that must come in every nation when times would not be so good as they were throughout the world between 1925 and 1930? But as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, one must not take hon. gentlemen opposite exactly at their word with regard to that $240,000,000, because, instead of cutting down the debt of Canada by $240,000,000 between 1925 and 1930, they added to the debt of the railways by $461,000,000. That is what they did. They added to the debt by $461,000,000, and if you take one from the other it leaves a net addition to the debt for which this country is responsible, although indirectly I admit, of $221,000,000 during that time. That is the actual fact.

speechtext: Certainly not, and no one knows better than the hon. gentleman, who is on the railway committee, that it was he and his friends on the other side of the house who put the railway into such a condition that they added to the debt of the railway in one year, as was so well pointed out by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Bey-non) in an outstandingly able speech to-day, not $205,000,000, as he said, but almost $250,000,000.

speechtext:
And you never opposed one
dollar of it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: One of our members stood up and did oppose it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: You did not.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I have admitted that in the house before. I did not understand it, but hon. gentlemen who were sitting in the government of that day, and who should have known better, permitted the Canadian National to be used as a pork barrel from the Atlantic to the Pacific, building hotels, terminals, branch lines, acquiring dead lines, building steamships and other things, to the amount of $250,000,000 in one year, or over two-thirds of the whole national debt of Canada before the war.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
And you never opened your
mouth about it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Maybe I did not open my mouth about it, but my hon. friend is very good at opening his.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I do not put my foot in mine like you do.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Well, I could put my foot in the hon. gentleman's-there is plenty of room.
Between 1926 and 1929 there was a boom and expansion throughout the world, and the revenues not only of this country but of every country were expanding. That was the time, if ever there was a time, when this country could easily have put into effect social legislation. I made inquiries two years ago of the bureau of statistics as to what were the total wages and salaries paid in Canada in 1931. That was not the boom year, but two years after the boom broke; and I found that the wages and salaries paid in this country-not the dividends and interest paid to the richer people-amounted to $2,500,000,000. One per cent of that would have created a fund each year of $25,000,000. If, as the Prime Minister pointed out the other day, hon. gentlemen opposite had put some legislation of this sort on the statute books at that time, as they should have done, we would have built up a fund of one or two hundred million dollars with which to help bridge over the depression when it came.
Mr. CAMPBEIiL: You were in power then.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
We were not in power
from 1925 to 1930.
Mr. CAMPBELiL: You were talking about 1931.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I was talking of the period from 1925 to 1930 when big revenues were coming in, and I say that in that period, at one per cent a fund could have been built ' up which would have helped us bridge over the depression.

speechtext:
You admit that we were
prosperous then.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes, but not because of
my hon. friends opposite. It was because the whole world was booming, and there was nothing that my hon. friend and his friends did to make us prosperous. On the contrary they did everything in their power, by allowing other countries to restrict their markets to us, to wreck this country in trade and everything else.
The right hon. leader of the opposition the other day spoke for two solid hours, and his lieutenants and supporters ever since have been giving constitutional reasons of all kinds, and various other reasons, why this legislation should not go into effect. They have proven through the Liberal convention and the reports of house committees in 1928 and 1929, and even by the book that the leader of the opposition wrote twenty years ago, that he has always stood for these principles, but he has never put them into practice. It reminds me of that rhyme-I may have forgotten the exact words, but it goes something like this:
For of all sad words of tongue or pen,
The saddest are these: "It might have been."

speechtext:
About ten years ago I
compared the leader of the opposition to Mr. Micawber. When Micawber owed a debt he always insisted on giving a promissory note and thanking God that the debt had been paid, and the leader of the opposition has been apparently under the impression for the last twenty years that so long as he put in books, in speeches, in charts and platforms, principles which he never lived up to when he got into power, the people ought to be satisfied and happy. He has been on all sides of all questions, and any one of us, the humblest member, can take that book which he wrote and which I tried to plough through some years ago, being unable to finish it- and I never met anyone but the leader of the opposition himself who did finish it-anyone, I say, can take that book and prove that the right hon. gentleman has been on all sides of all questions at all times in any period in the last twenty years.

You have been on two sides
of the reciprocity question.

speechtext: Take it back.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
There is nothing to take
back; I did not compare the right hon. gentleman to Hauptmann. My hon. friends are a little too thin skinned, after some of the remarks they have addressed to this side of the house.
I simply wish to point out that the Liberal party, ever since this measure was introduced, has been pretending cooperation and really opposing the measure. They have done as they have usually done with all the measures which we have introduced at any time in the last four years; they have been fault finding, opposing and offering destructive criticism. They have stood up when they thought it good politics and said, "We are for these measures;" but they put every obstacle in the way of getting these measures on the statute books. They forget that the world throughout the last four years has passed through one of the most terrible crises in its history. They forget that there have been thirty million unemployed, of which number Canada has had but a very, very small proportion, about one or two per cent. In all the industrial countries of the world there have been some thirty millions unemployed, and two-thirds of the world's trade has been cut off by the depression. But my hon. friends have deemed it sufficient for them to play politics, placing party first and the state second. Macaulay once said that none was for the party and all were for the state; but on the other side all are for the party and' none is for the state. And that has been so throughout the whole four years. In

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
my opinion the people of this country realize that the Prime Minister has had the vision and the courage to recognize the necessity for correcting the errors of our system. Anyone who is not totally blind and deaf knows that the system under which we live has very serious errors. No system under which young men and young women, boys and girls coming out of our schools and colleges, find it impossible to get work; no system under which there are hundreds of thousands of people who are willing to work and unable to get work, who cannot earn the necessaries of life for their loved ones; no system that permits that condition is a good system. The system should be corrected, and my right hon. leader, the Prime Minister, is attempting to correct these errors from within. But my hon. friends are doing everything they can to prevent the system being corrected-what for? For purposes of party politics and nothing else. The leader of the opposition says that this measure will do nothing for those who are at present unemployed and that we are not worrying about the future. That is another attempt to capitalize discontent. Have we had any support from him during the last four years, and particularly during the last year, when we supplied $40,000,000 for public works?

speechtext: We voted for it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: You may have voted for it but you talked against it. My hon. friends usually get in line and vote for what looks good politically, but they always stand up and oppose everything that is brought forward. We looked after the drought area in Saskatchewan, where there were 300,000 people on relief. This government took care of them and received little thanks from the members from Saskatchewan on the other side. We took care of camps for the young and we were accused of setting up slave camps for these young people. And we have safeguarded the credit of the country. Practically every measure of a constructive kind which this government has brought forward in the last four years, and particularly during the last year, has met with fault finding and destructive criticism on the other side:-in other words, party politics. That is what we have been receiving from the other side. They have been sitting by hoping that something would turn up to keep the depression going until an election came around, hoping that they would float into power on a tide of discontent.
